family: Linux networking: NAPI IRQ/poll switching and budget, software IRQ deferral (napi_defer_hard_irqs + gro_flush_timeout), busy polling (SO_BUSY_POLL, busy_read/busy_poll, epoll EPIOCSPARAMS, prefer_busy_poll, threaded busy poll), IRQ suspension (irq_suspend_timeout, Damato & Karsten, kernel 6.13+) and its paper (Cai & Karsten, SIGMETRICS'24), net DIM (lib/dim: net_dim, rdma_dim, mlx5 use), and driver adaptive ITR (ixgbe, igb)

mechanisms.name: NAPI IRQ->poll switch with per-poll weight and per-softirq budget
mechanisms.where: Local 6.8.12 tree /home/jetson/src/l4t-r39.2.1/Linux_for_Tegra/source/kernel/kernel-noble: include/linux/netdevice.h:2698 (NAPI_POLL_WEIGHT), net/core/dev.c:4545-4547 (netdev_budget, netdev_budget_usecs), dev.c:6868 net_rx_action, dev.c:6210 napi_complete_done, kernel/softirq.c:512-513. Live sysctls on this board: netdev_budget=300, netdev_budget_usecs=8000.
mechanisms.algorithm: The hard IRQ masks the device IRQ and calls napi_schedule. In softirq, net_rx_action takes the per-CPU poll_list and calls each napi->poll(budget = weight, default NAPI_POLL_WEIGHT 64). If the driver does work < weight, it calls napi_complete_done() and re-arms the device IRQ (back to interrupt mode). If work == weight, the instance stays in poll mode and is put on the repoll list. Whole-softirq limits: budget netdev_budget=300 packets, time limit jiffies + usecs_to_jiffies(netdev_budget_usecs), default 2*USEC_PER_SEC/HZ. On this board that is 8000 us (HZ=250, CONFIG_HZ=250 confirmed). Source comment: 'Allow this to run for 2 jiffies since which will allow an average latency of 1.5/HZ.' On exhaustion it does sd->time_squeeze++ (an overload counter, shown in /proc/net/softnet_stat), re-raises NET_RX_SOFTIRQ and returns. The generic softirq loop restarts at most MAX_SOFTIRQ_RESTART=10 times or for MAX_SOFTIRQ_TIME=2 ms, then defers to ksoftirqd, an ordinary CFS/EEVDF thread that competes fairly with user load. In napi_complete_done, NAPIF_STATE_MISSED (an IRQ arrived while polling) makes it reschedule instead of re-arming, which closes the race between 'queue empty' and 're-enable IRQ'.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Analogy: 'packet' = host-call request, 'IRQ mode' = the watcher's slow tier, 'poll mode' = the hot tier (spin, WFE or short sleep). (1) Exit hot mode on the first empty poll (work < weight), not after a fixed 200 us as policy N does. (2) Cap each hot episode by count and by time (the netdev_budget / netdev_budget_usecs analog), then do a voluntary sleep, the ksoftirqd hand-off analog. Under EEVDF, a thread that sleeps often keeps positive lag and gets picked quickly when it wakes. A thread that spins through its slice gets preempted for about a tick (4 ms at HZ=250). That matches the 13-31% of W calls that waited >1 ms under 6-thread load. (3) The MISSED-bit race exists for us too: after deciding to sleep, re-check flag1 once before sleeping. The cost is one load (~0). (4) A time_squeeze analog is a counter of hot episodes that hit the time cap. Use it as the overload signal that turns hot mode off. Signals: consecutive empty polls, plus whether a hot episode hit its cap. Both are free.
mechanisms.measured: No published numbers in the source. The 1.5/HZ latency figure is a code comment.

mechanisms.name: Software IRQ deferral: napi_defer_hard_irqs + gro_flush_timeout
mechanisms.where: net/core/dev.c:6210-6279 napi_complete_done (local 6.8.12). The same logic is at mainline 7.4-rc2 net/core/dev.c:7004 (fetched 2026-11-11 to /tmp/claude-2002/-home-jetson-src/6ac0883f-4479-466c-bec5-5fa31cffe4de/scratchpad/src/net_core_dev.c). napi_watchdog is at dev.c:~6455 local, 7380 mainline. Doc: https://docs.kernel.org/networking/napi.html ('Software IRQ coalescing'). Added in 5.10 (version from memory, not checked against git). Per-NAPI netlink config (napi-set defer-hard-irqs / gro-flush-timeout) arrived in 6.13 per the netdev 0x19 slides.
mechanisms.algorithm: In napi_complete_done(n, work_done): if work_done > 0, reload n->defer_hard_irqs_count = dev->napi_defer_hard_irqs (and timeout = gro_flush_timeout if GRO is active). Then, if defer_hard_irqs_count > 0: decrement it, timeout = gro_flush_timeout (ns), and when timeout != 0 return false. Returning false means the driver must NOT re-enable the device IRQ. Clear SCHED, then hrtimer_start(&n->timer, timeout ns, HRTIMER_MODE_REL_PINNED). When the timer fires, napi_watchdog() does test_and_set SCHED, clears PREFER_BUSY_POLL and calls __napi_schedule_irqoff, so the poll runs again from the timer. The result is periodic timer polling. Any poll that finds work refills the counter. After napi_defer_hard_irqs consecutive empty polls the IRQ is re-armed. Doc: 'napi_defer_hard_irqs controls the number of consecutive empty polls before NAPI gives up and goes back to using hardware IRQs.' Units: count, and nanoseconds for gro_flush_timeout. Defaults are 0/0, i.e. off. On this board all NICs show 0/0, except wlP1p1s0 with gro_flush_timeout=100000 and defer 0, so its timer does not drive polling.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the closest kernel analog of what policy N / M100 already does. The difference is in how the policy leaves the busy state: NAPI counts K consecutive empty timer polls at a fixed short period, instead of using a time window plus exponential back-off. Concrete rule: after any served request, set k = K and period = P. Each wake sleeps P us (slack 1 us, so it lasts P+4 us). A wake that finds a request sets k = K again. An empty wake does k--. At k = 0, drop to the slow tier (M100 or the 1 ms cap). Example: K=10, P=20 us gives a ~240 us busy window, comparable to N's 200 us hot spin. CPU cost is K x 1.2 us = 12 us per idle-out instead of ~200 us of spinning. Expected wait inside the window is ~P/2+4 us. Signal: whether each wake found a request (free). Cost on this board: 1.2 us CPU per wake. Between bursts the CPU cost is the same as the slow tier (M100: +33-61 mW). Inside a burst, P=10-50 us costs what S10/S50 cost while active (+200 / +70 mW) but only for K wakes. Under full load the measurements say shorter periods get worse, so P should grow when the overload signal fires (see the IRQ suspension and busy-poll entries).
mechanisms.measured: Kernel doc: no numbers. Cover letter (see the IRQ suspension entry), 200K qps memcached: base avg/95/99 = 112/237/415 at 26% CPU; defer10 (defer 100, gro 10 us) = 54/123/142 at 28% CPU. Latency units are not stated in the letter; they are probably us (Mutilate), inferred, not verified.

mechanisms.name: Socket/epoll busy polling (SO_BUSY_POLL, net.core.busy_read, net.core.busy_poll, EPIOCSPARAMS)
mechanisms.where: include/net/busy_poll.h (local 6.8.12): BUSY_POLL_BUDGET 8, busy_loop_current_time, busy_loop_timeout, sk_busy_loop. net/core/dev.c:~6347 napi_busy_loop. net/core/sock.c:4175 sk_busy_loop_end, sock.c:3520 (sk_ll_usec = sysctl_net_busy_read). fs/eventpoll.c:391-422. Mainline 7.4-rc2 fs/eventpoll.c:649-690 (ep_busy_loop_on, ep_busy_loop) plus the EPIOCSPARAMS ioctl (doc says 'recent kernels'; 6.9 is from memory, not verified). Board: CONFIG_NET_RX_BUSY_POLL=y, busy_read=busy_poll=0.
mechanisms.algorithm: When a blocking recv/poll/epoll_wait finds nothing and busy polling is enabled for the socket/epoll, napi_busy_loop(napi_id, loop_end, ...) runs with preemption disabled. Each iteration: claim the NAPI (cmpxchg SCHED|IN_BUSY_POLL; if another context owns it, just count), call napi->poll(budget) with budget = SO_BUSY_POLL_BUDGET or BUSY_POLL_BUDGET = 8 (epoll default 8; >64 needs CAP_NET_ADMIN), then check loop_end. loop_end is true when data or events are available, or when now > start + usec. Time is ktime_get_ns() >> 10, so the 'usec' unit is really 1.024 us. If need_resched() is set, it calls busy_poll_stop(), re-enables preemption, cond_resched(), and restarts unless loop_end is now true. Otherwise cpu_relax() and loop. busy_poll_stop() clears MISSED/IN_BUSY_POLL and calls napi->poll once more to re-arm the IRQ (without prefer_busy_poll). When the epoll busy loop times out with no events, it sets ep->napi_id = 0 and does not busy poll again until a socket with a valid NAPI id puts an event on the ready list. Knobs: busy_read = default per-socket spin for read; busy_poll = spin for poll/select/epoll; the EPIOCSPARAMS struct is {u32 busy_poll_usecs; u16 busy_poll_budget; u8 prefer_busy_poll; u8 __pad}.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Mapping: busy_poll_usecs = the hot-spin length B after a request. 'Socket has a napi_id' = 'a probed kernel is in flight' (the CUDA launch hook). 'ep->napi_id = 0 after an empty spin, re-learned on the next event' = drop hot mode after an empty spin and re-arm it only when a request arrives. That avoids polling CUDA events every 100 us, which was measured as not paying off when the GPU is ~100% busy. need_resched has no user-space equivalent. Substitutes: (a) wake lateness = actual sleep - requested sleep - 4 us, free because the watcher already timestamps; (b) delta of run_delay (field 2 of /proc/thread-self/schedstat, ns), with the fd kept open and re-read by pread (rough Python-level check on this board: ~1.1 us per pread, ~34 us if reopened each time; indicative only, not a benchmark); (c) getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD).ru_nivcsw delta (cost not measured). If the signal shows preemption, end the spin and sleep, like the cond_resched path. Cost: spinning is ~1 core per spinning us. N's 200 us window is this mechanism with B=200. The ~1.024-us unit detail is irrelevant for us.
mechanisms.measured: Cover letter 'napibusy' (defer 100, gro 200 us, busy_poll_usecs 64, budget 64, prefer): 200K load 100/237/275 at 56% CPU vs base 112/237/415 at 26%. At MAX load, napibusy has the worst tail: 99% = 10753 vs base 5743. Units probably us (inferred).

mechanisms.name: Preferred busy polling (SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL / epoll prefer_busy_poll)
mechanisms.where: net/core/dev.c busy_poll_stop (local ~6303; mainline 7.4-rc2 7118), napi_busy_loop sets NAPI_STATE_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, mainline __napi_poll ~8011 early exit, napi_watchdog clears the bit. Doc section 'IRQ mitigation'. Added in 5.11 (from memory, not verified).
mechanisms.algorithm: With prefer_busy_poll, busy_poll_stop() does not call napi->poll to re-enable the IRQ. It sets defer_hard_irqs_count = napi_defer_hard_irqs, and if that and gro_flush_timeout are both non-zero, it arms the hrtimer for gro_flush_timeout. Local 6.8 still calls poll but sets skip_schedule; mainline clears SCHED and only starts the timer. So the device IRQ stays masked and the timer is the only backstop. A busy-poller that finds the NAPI owned by softirq sets PREFER_BUSY_POLL, and __napi_poll then completes early instead of repolling in softirq, which hands the queue to the app thread. The 'pledge' is revoked if gro_flush_timeout passes with no busy-poll call: the watchdog fires, clears PREFER_BUSY_POLL and schedules normal NAPI. Doc: 'choosing a large value for gro_flush_timeout will defer IRQs ... but will induce latency when the system is not fully loaded. Choosing a small value ... can cause interference ... by device IRQs and softirq processing.'
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The application declares that it will poll, and the kernel then stops interrupting it but keeps a timer backstop. Our analog of the app's opt-in is the CUDA context scheduling flag. Read it once at attach via cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState. CU_CTX_SCHED_SPIN means the app has already accepted burning a core, so W/hot spin may be used during probed kernels. BLOCKING_SYNC or AUTO (which behaves as blocking on this Orin) means default to timer-only tiers, matching the kernel default busy_poll=0. Cost: one driver call per context, ~0 per request. The timer backstop is the same structure as the slow tier. Revoke-on-silence = leave the hot tier after gro_flush_timeout without a request.
mechanisms.measured: No standalone numbers. It is part of the napibusy/fullbusy/suspend configurations in the cover letter.

mechanisms.name: IRQ suspension (irq_suspend_timeout), Damato & Karsten, merged for 6.13
mechanisms.where: Mainline 7.4-rc2 (fetched 2026-11-11): net/core/dev.c:7284 napi_suspend_irqs, :7300 napi_resume_irqs; fs/eventpoll.c:2229-2242 ep_try_send_events, :668-690 ep_busy_loop, :773-787 ep_suspend/resume_napi_irqs, :1056 ep_free. Doc: https://docs.kernel.org/networking/napi.html ('IRQ suspension'). Cover letter v6: https://lists.openwall.net/netdev/2024/11/04/303 = https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/2411.0/03929.html. Slides: netdevconf 0x19, Joe Damato, 'IRQ Suspension: a new, efficient mechanism for packet delivery' (says kernel 6.13+). Not present in the local 6.8 tree.
mechanisms.algorithm: Per-NAPI parameter irq_suspend_timeout (ns, netlink napi-set 'irq-suspend-timeout'). Active only when it is non-zero and the epoll context has prefer_busy_poll=1. State machine as coded: (1) ep_try_send_events: if ep_send_events returns > 0 events, then napi_suspend_irqs(napi_id) = hrtimer_start(&napi->timer, irq_suspend_timeout, REL_PINNED). That replaces any pending gro_flush_timeout timer, so IRQs stay masked and the deadline moves out on every non-empty return. (2) ep_busy_loop: napi_busy_loop(... prefer, budget); if events are now available, return; otherwise, with prefer_busy_poll, call napi_resume_irqs = napi_schedule(napi), which runs a normal NAPI poll that ends in napi_complete_done. There the defer_hard_irqs/gro_flush_timeout logic takes over (timer polling for K empty polls, then IRQ re-arm). Then ep->napi_id = 0. (3) busy_poll_stop with prefer arms the gro_flush_timeout timer instead of re-enabling the IRQ. (4) Safety: if the app does not call epoll_wait again within irq_suspend_timeout, the watchdog fires and normal NAPI processing resumes. Doc: 'During busy periods, irq-suspend-timeout overrides gro_flush_timeout and keeps the system busy polling, but when epoll finds no events, the setting of gro_flush_timeout and napi_defer_hard_irqs determine the next step.' 'Setting gro_flush_timeout and napi_defer_hard_irqs is the recommended usage, because otherwise setting irq-suspend-timeout might not have any discernible effect.' Recommended setup (slides): busy_poll_usecs=0, busy_poll_budget<=64, prefer_busy_poll=1, defer-hard-irqs ~10, gro-flush-timeout ~20000 ns, irq-suspend-timeout = maximum time the app needs to process one epoll_wait batch. Cover-letter configs: suspendX = defer 100, gro X us, irq_suspend_timeout 20,000,000 ns (20 ms), busy_poll_usecs 0, budget 64, prefer true; suspend0 = defer 0, gro 0, suspend 20 ms.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is a three-tier policy driven by 'did the last look find work'. It maps directly onto warp bursts (32 lanes ~9 us apart) and onto the measured trade-off. Tier A, 'suspended' = hot: spin/WFE while each check finds a request. Every served request re-arms a deadline D (the irq_suspend_timeout analog, ~one warp burst = 32 x 9 ≈ 300 us; it bounds CPU if the GPU stalls mid-burst). Tier B, deferral: on the first empty check (in practice a gap > ~2-3 x 9 us, since lanes arrive ~9 us apart), switch to K short sleeps of P us, from the defer/gro entry. Tier C: slow tier (M100/1 ms). The lessons transfer directly. suspend0 ≈ base: without tier B, tier A gains nothing, so a hot tier needs a short-timer fallback. suspend10 vs suspend200 at 200K: 53 vs 149 avg latency for 32% vs 20% CPU. That is the same knob as our S10 (22 us, +200 mW) vs M100 (66 us, +33-61 mW), i.e. P sets the latency/CPU trade. Using the request itself as the re-arm event replaces 100-us CUDA-event polling (measured as costing more than it saves at ~100% GPU busy). Launch hooks only decide whether tier B may be entered at all (probed kernel in flight). Cost: tier A is hot spin/WFE only for the length of a burst (≤ D), so its CPU scales with burst time, not with kernel run time. That limits the 14% load loss measured for W, which held the core for the whole kernel. Under load (wake lateness or run_delay rising), skip tier A, because spinning is what gets preempted for a tick.
mechanisms.measured: Cover letter (AMD EPYC 7662, 64 cores, ConnectX-5 100G, 8 RX queues, memcached + mutilate; columns qps, avg, 95%, 99%, cpu%; latency unit not stated, probably us): MAX load: base 1054805 qps 4152/5298/5743; fullbusy 1248006 3472/3918/3979; suspend20 1226845 3514/3939/3985; suspend0 1034456 4242/5668/6042. 200K: base 112/237/415 at 26%; defer10 54/123/142 at 28%; fullbusy 46/117/132 at 100%; suspend10 53/123/141 at 32%; suspend200 149/250/302 at 20%. 400K: base 139/268/715 at 40%; defer20 66/140/171 at 47%; suspend20 61/135/167 at 49%; suspend200 154/267/325 at 34%. 800K: base 179/298/555 at 86%; napibusy 65/142/216 at 99%; suspend20 74/151/209 at 79%; suspend200 160/292/357 at 62%. 1000K: base 3498/5740/6239 at 97%; suspend10 80/162/222 at 92%; suspend200 163/298/363 at 76%.

mechanisms.name: Kernel Polling (paper prototype of IRQ suspension)
mechanisms.where: Peter Cai, Martin Karsten, 'Kernel vs. User-Level Networking: Don't Throw Out the Stack with the Interrupts', Proc. ACM Meas. Anal. Comput. Syst. 7(3) Art. 49, Dec 2023 (SIGMETRICS 2024), doi 10.1145/3626780. Preprint https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~mkarsten/papers/sigmetrics2024-preprint.pdf (read locally: /tmp/claude-2002/-home-jetson-src/6ac0883f-4479-466c-bec5-5fa31cffe4de/scratchpad/napi_paper/karsten.txt), Sections 4.2-4.3 and Fig. 4.
mechanisms.algorithm: Fig. 4 ep_poll: avail = events_available; loop { if avail { events = get_events; if events[0].napi_id != ep.last_napi_id then unmask_interrupts(last); last = new; mask_interrupts(last); return events } avail = do_busy_poll(ep); if avail continue; unmask_interrupts(last); sleep_until_notified(ep); avail = events_available }. 'The relevant IRQs stay masked until a subsequent epoll_wait() call comes up empty'. About 30 lines of kernel change. The prototype had no timeout. The paper proposes 'a kernel timeout set on the return path from epoll_wait()' as the production fallback, which became irq_suspend_timeout. Ideal setup: a 1:1 mapping of app threads to RX queues via SO_INCOMING_NAPI_ID. The paper also rejects 'IRQ suppression' (huge NIC coalescing values plus busy poll) as needing 'meticulous tuning for each application and ... each workload situation'.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Core principle: an event source should not interrupt the consumer while the consumer has work, and should fall back to the cheap notification path only when a check comes up empty. For the watcher, the 'interrupt' is the timer wake-up and the 'work' is a pending request. During a warp burst, do not go back to timed sleeps between lanes; just re-check. The paper's rejection of static big-coalescing settings is the networking version of our finding that no fixed period wins at both idle and full load. 1:1 thread-to-queue corresponds to one watcher per shared-memory slot/context. Cost: none beyond the IRQ suspension entry.
mechanisms.measured: Abstract/conclusion: up to 45% higher throughput (NUMA) and 30% (UMA) for memcached vs vanilla Linux 'without compromising tail latency'. Hardware: 2x Xeon E5-2680 (16 cores), ConnectX-3 10GbE.

mechanisms.name: Threaded NAPI busy poll (napi kthread spins)
mechanisms.where: Doc https://docs.kernel.org/networking/napi.html 'Threaded NAPI busy polling'. Mainline 7.4-rc2 net/core/dev.c:7446 (NETDEV_NAPI_THREADED_BUSY_POLL), :8087 napi_threaded_poll_loop. Exact merge version not verified (newer than 6.13).
mechanisms.algorithm: Enable with netlink napi-set {threaded: 'busy-poll'}. The napi/<if>-<id> kthread polls continuously. It calls cond_resched() on repoll and reports RCU quiescent states via busy_poll_last_qs. Doc: 'Note that this will keep the CPU core busy with 100% usage', and recommends pinning the kthread to an unused CPU.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the kernel's version of policy W or a pinned hot spinner. Linux ships it only as an explicit opt-in that dedicates a core. That matches our measurement: W costs 14% of a 6-thread CPU-bound load even when probes never call the host, and 13-31% of calls wait >1 ms when it is preempted. So it should be gated on an explicit signal (CU_CTX_SCHED_SPIN or an env knob) and ideally an isolated core. Not the default.
mechanisms.measured: No numbers in the doc.

mechanisms.name: net DIM (lib/dim/net_dim.c): stats-driven hill climbing over 5 moderation profiles
mechanisms.where: Local 6.8.12: lib/dim/net_dim.c (profiles, net_dim_step, net_dim_stats_compare, net_dim_decision, net_dim), lib/dim/dim.c (dim_on_top, dim_turn, dim_park_on_top/tired, dim_calc_stats), include/linux/dim.h:17 DIM_NEVENTS, :23 IS_SIGNIFICANT_DIFF. Mainline 7.4-rc2 uses the same decision logic and adds user-configurable profiles (net_dim_init_irq_moder, rx/tx_profile per dev) and u64 math in dim_calc_stats. Driver use: drivers/net/ethernet/mellanox/mlx5/core/en_txrx.c:61-71 mlx5e_handle_rx_dim, called at :234 after napi_complete_done and before mlx5e_cq_arm. en_dim.c mlx5e_rx_dim_work applies the profile via mlx5_core_modify_cq_moderation(usec, pkts) and sets state = DIM_START_MEASURE. en_main.c:5026 rx_dim_enabled = MLX5_CAP_GEN(cq_moderation), i.e. adaptive-rx is on by default when the HW can do it.
mechanisms.algorithm: Profiles {usec, pkts}: RX EQE-mode {1,256},{8,256},{64,256},{128,256},{256,256}; RX CQE-mode {2,256},{8,128},{16,64},{32,64},{64,64}; TX EQE {1,128},{8,128},{32,128},{64,128},{128,128}; TX CQE {5,128},{8,64},{16,32},{32,32},{64,32}. Start index 1. Index 0 = least moderation, 'going right' = more. Sampling: each NAPI completion passes (event_ctr, packets, bytes). Once ≥ DIM_NEVENTS = 64 events since start_sample, compute rates per ms over the elapsed time: ppms, bpms, epms = 64*1000/delta_us (events per ms), cpms. Compare to prev_stats in this order: bpms (higher better), then ppms (higher better), then epms (lower better). Each needs IS_SIGNIFICANT_DIFF = |curr-prev|*100/prev > 10 (%), else SAME. If prev is 0: BETTER if curr is non-zero, else SAME. Decision: GOING_LEFT/RIGHT: if result != BETTER then dim_turn (reverse; zero the new direction's step count). If dim_on_top (going right with steps_left > 1 && steps_right == 1, or the mirror case, i.e. it just stepped one back after a run the other way) then park_on_top. Else step: at the edge (index 0 or 4) park_on_top. If tired == 2*5 = 10 steps, park_tired. Otherwise index±1, tired++. PARKING_ON_TOP: stay until compare != SAME (any >10% change), then exit parking (go left if index > 0, else right) and step. PARKING_TIRED: tired-- each window, and exit parking at 0, so it rests about 10 windows. prev_stats is updated every window except while staying parked on top. When the index changes, state = APPLY_NEW_PROFILE and schedule_work runs the driver callback in a workqueue (asynchronous). Measurement restarts only after the work resets the state to START_MEASURE.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Map the profile array to a small set of sleep periods, e.g. {10, 20, 50, 100, 1000} us (index 0 = lowest latency). event = one watcher wake-up; packets = requests served; bytes = none (skip bpms). Because GPU host calls are synchronous (each lane waits for flag2 and then issues the next), request throughput is closed-loop: when latency drops, ppms rises. So 'ppms higher is better, then epms (wakes per ms) lower is better' is the right objective for us without changes, and the >10% band plus tired parking stop oscillation. Window: 64 wakes = 0.9 ms at P=10, 6.4 ms at P=100, 64 ms at 1 ms. A full search of ≤10 steps therefore takes ~10-100 ms while active, which is fine for long kernels. At idle, ppms = 0 on both sides, so it parks (SAME) and costs nothing. Caveat: with entry/exit probes only (a few requests per launch), ppms is mostly set by the workload, not by us, so the controller wanders inside the 10% band. Gate it on the burst case (a request seen in the last window). Apply can be synchronous for us (just a variable), so there is no workqueue delay. Cost: a few integer ops per wake (~0) plus clock_gettime once per 64 wakes. It does not detect CPU contention, because higher latency from preemption simply looks 'worse' and it moves toward the shortest period, which the board data says is wrong under load. So it needs an overload guard (wake lateness / run_delay) that forces right moves.
mechanisms.measured: No numbers in the source. Mellanox/NVIDIA DIM papers or talks were not located or verified.

mechanisms.name: RDMA DIM (lib/dim/rdma_dim.c): completions-per-event objective
mechanisms.where: Local 6.8.12 lib/dim/rdma_dim.c. include/linux/dim.h:322-323 RDMA_DIM_PARAMS_NUM_PROFILES 9, RDMA_DIM_START_PROFILE 0. Profiles in drivers/infiniband/core/cq.c:27-37.
mechanisms.algorithm: 9 profiles {usec, -, comps}: {1,1},{1,4},{2,4},{2,8},{4,8},{16,8},{16,16},{32,16},{32,32}. Called once per CQ event with the completion count. After 64 events: cpms = completions per ms, cpe_ratio = cpms*100/epms (completions per event x100). Compare: if prev cpms == 0, SAME. Else significant (>10%) cpms change decides (higher better), else significant cpe_ratio change (higher better), else SAME. Decision: SAME and cpe_ratio <= 50*prev_ix: reset to profile 0 (snap back to lowest latency when batching is low). WORSE: turn, then step. BETTER: step. At the edge it turns. It has no parking and no tired logic.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: cpe_ratio maps exactly to 'requests per wake-up', i.e. the hit ratio, since the single request slot gives at most 1 request per wake. The 'snap to profile 0 when cpe_ratio is low' rule is the opposite of what we want: a low hit ratio means we wake too often, so lengthen the period. The usable part is the signal: hit ratio h = requests/wakes per 64-wake window, a free counter. Pair it with the square-root rule: the optimal period scales as 1/sqrt(rate), so with rate λ ≈ h/P, choose P_new = sqrt(2c/(αλ)), with c = 1.2 us of wake CPU on this board.

mechanisms.name: ixgbe adaptive ITR (ethtool adaptive-rx on Intel 10G)
mechanisms.where: Local 6.8.12 drivers/net/ethernet/intel/ixgbe/ixgbe.h:469-473, 545-548; ixgbe_main.c:2535 ixgbe_update_itr, :2748 ixgbe_set_itr (called from ixgbe_poll at :3430 when the poll completes).
mechanisms.algorithm: Constants: MIN_INC 2, MIN_USECS 10, MAX_USECS 126, LATENCY flag 0x80, BULK 0x00. The interrupt-delay in us is q_vector->itr >> 2. Each update: if more than 1 jiffy has passed since next_update (next_update = jiffies + 1, i.e. the window is 1-2 jiffies = 4-8 ms at HZ=250), reset to itr = 10 us | LATENCY (traffic is too slow or NAPI is already polling). Else, with packets/bytes since the last update: packets == 0 gives itr = cur + 2 (cap 126), keeping the LATENCY flag. packets < 4 && bytes < 9000 gives LATENCY mode and goes to the size formula. packets < 48: cur + 2, cap 126 (delay slightly too low, so increase). 48 ≤ packets < 96: keep cur ('goldilocks'). 96 ≤ packets < 256: cur/2, floor 10 ('slight overrun of the delay', so halve). ≥ 256: BULK, size formula. Size formula on avg = bytes/packets: ≤60 → 5120; ≤316 → avg*40+2720; ≤1084 → avg*15+11452; <1968 → avg*5+22420; else 32256. Halve it in LATENCY mode. At 10G: itr += ceil(v/(2*256))*2; at 1G/2.5G: min(v, 8064), then itr += ceil(v/(2*64))*2. new_itr = min(rx, tx) with the flag stripped. Write EITR only if it changed.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The usable part is the AIMD shape on the delay with no extra signals. Target a fixed number of events per interrupt window: too few → +2 us, too many → halve, plus a fast reset to the minimum when the history is stale. Since our slot holds at most one request, use per-wake hit/miss instead of packet counts. On a hit (request found), P = max(P/2, Pmin = 10 us). On a miss, P = min(P + δ, Pmax): δ around 2-10 us within a probed kernel, Pmax = 100 us (M100), and 1 ms outside probed kernels. Reset rule analog: if no wake for more than 1-2 'windows' (e.g. after a long sleep), restart at Pmin only if a launch hook says a probed kernel just started; otherwise stay at Pmax. Cost: 0 extra signals, 1.2 us per wake. Expected behavior: within a warp burst P collapses toward 10 us (S10 latency ~22 us only while the burst lasts). Between bursts it climbs back to 100 us (M100 power) in (100-10)/δ misses. The 1-2 jiffy window is far too coarse for us; express windows in wakes, not ticks.

mechanisms.name: igb adaptive ITR (3-state classifier, InterruptThrottleRate dynamic/conservative)
mechanisms.where: Local 6.8.12 drivers/net/ethernet/intel/igb/igb_main.c:5841 igb_update_itr, :5893 igb_set_itr; igb.h:29-32 (IGB_START_ITR 648 ~6000/s, IGB_4K_ITR 980, IGB_20K_ITR 196, IGB_70K_ITR 56).
mechanisms.algorithm: States lowest_latency (70,000 ints/s), low_latency (20,000/s), bulk_latency (4,000/s). Per window of packets/bytes (skipped if packets == 0): from lowest, bytes/packets > 8000 → bulk; packets < 5 && bytes > 512 → low. From low: if bytes > 10000 { bytes/packets > 8000 → bulk; packets < 10 or bytes/packets > 1200 → bulk; packets > 35 → lowest }, else if bytes/packets > 2000 → bulk, else if packets ≤ 2 && bytes < 512 → lowest. From bulk: bytes > 25000 && packets > 35 → low; bytes < 1500 → low. Uses max(rx, tx) state. Conservative mode (itr setting 3) replaces lowest with low. Non-1G links are fixed at 4K. Smoothing when the delay increases: new = max(new*old/(new + old/4), new). My own arithmetic: for new > old, new*old/(new+old/4) < old < new, so max() always returns new and the smoothing never takes effect.

Moving one tier at a time with different up/down thresholds avoids flapping. Its smoothing line is effectively dead code, so do not copy it. Cost: ~0 per wake.

Analogy used throughout: packet = host-call request; device IRQ / 'IRQ mode' = the watcher's cheap slow tier. The GPU cannot interrupt the CPU, so the slow timed sleep is our interrupt fallback. Composite design implied by this family (not measured):
- Tier A (IRQ-suspension style): after a served request, re-check without sleeping (or WFE) while each check finds a request, with a re-armed deadline D ≈ one warp burst (~300 us).
- Tier B (defer_hard_irqs + gro_flush_timeout style): on the first empty check, do K short sleeps of P us (e.g. K=10, P=20, about 12 us CPU per idle-out), refilling K on any hit. P is adapted by ixgbe-style AIMD (halve on hit, +δ on miss) or by a DIM-style search with objective requests/ms, then wakes/ms.
- Tier C: M100/1 ms slow tier, the IRQ-re-armed analog.
- Overload guard (need_resched / time_squeeze analog): wake lateness (free) or the run_delay delta from schedstat. When either rises, skip tier A and raise P, since the board data show shorter periods and spinning lose under full load (W: -14% load, 13-31% of calls >1 ms; M100 best at full load).
- Opt-in for permanent hot polling (prefer_busy_poll / threaded busy-poll analog): the CUDA context flag CU_CTX_SCHED_SPIN via cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState. AUTO behaves as blocking on this Orin, so the default stays timer-based.
- Launch hooks gate entry into tier B, which replaces 100-us CUDA-event polling.

The cover-letter results (suspend0 ≈ base; suspend10 vs suspend200 = latency vs CPU) are the networking evidence that the hot tier only helps with a short-timer middle tier, and that the middle tier's period is the knob that trades latency for CPU, the same as our S10 vs M100.

mechanisms.name: blk-mq classic polling (Linux 4.4+), and its structural lesson: the poll loop exits when need_resched()
mechanisms.where: Introduced by Jens Axboe in commit 05229beeddf7 'block: add block polling support' (2015-11-05, https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/05229beeddf7e75e2e616ddaad4b70e7fca9528d). Current loop in the local 6.8 tree: /home/jetson/src/l4t-r39.2.1/Linux_for_Tegra/source/kernel/kernel-noble/block/blk-mq.c:5016-5041 (blk_hctx_poll). v5.15 version: blk_poll() in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v5.15/block/blk-mq.c (around line 3965).
mechanisms.algorithm: do { ret = q->mq_ops->poll(hctx, iob); if (ret>0) return ret; if (signal_pending_state) set RUNNING; if (task_is_running(current)) return 1; if (ret<0 || flags&BLK_POLL_ONESHOT) break; cpu_relax(); } while (!need_resched()); There is no timeout and no sleep. The only things that stop the spin are a completion, a signal, a ONESHOT flag (io_uring with several devices or a non-spinning caller), or need_resched(), meaning the scheduler wants this CPU for another task. In v5.15, the counters hctx->poll_considered, poll_invoked and poll_success were kept for debugfs.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Our policy W (WFE on flag1) is classic polling with a power hint. What W lacks is the need_resched() exit. A kernel poller gives up the CPU the moment another task is runnable on that CPU. A user-space WFE loop gets no such signal and is only preempted at a tick (HZ=250, so 4 ms). That explains the measured 14% load loss and the 13-31% of calls waiting more than 1 ms. A user-space stand-in for need_resched(): (a) after every WFE wake (at least every ~100 us through evtstrm), read the CLOCK_MONOTONIC gap. A jump much larger than 100 us means we were descheduled. This costs nothing (vDSO). (b) Every ~1-10 ms, read field 2 (run_delay, ns) of /proc/thread-self/schedstat, or call getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD) and read ru_nivcsw. A growing value means the CPU is contended, so leave WFE mode and drop to M100. I checked this board: CONFIG_SCHED_INFO=y and CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS=y, so schedstat works. CONFIG_PSI is not set, so /proc/pressure is absent and PSI cannot be the signal. Cost: one open/read/parse of the procfs file, a few us, which I have not measured on this board. Amortised over 1-10 ms it is under 0.1% of a core.
mechanisms.measured: FAST'12 (Yang et al.): synchronous polled 4 KiB read 4.4 us vs 7.6 us with interrupts; polled IOPS up to 2M on 8 CPUs, and the async path reached only 60-70% of that. HotStorage'22 (Optane 900P, kernel 5.15.16): classic poll 8.1 us / 120,470 IOPS at 1 thread vs IRQ 10.1 us / 96,722.

mechanisms.name: blk-mq hybrid polling: fixed delay and adaptive 'half the mean' (io_poll_delay; Linux 4.10 to 6.3)
mechanisms.where: Patchset cover letter, Axboe 2016-11-01 'block: IO polling improvements' (https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1611.0/00460.html). Commit 06426adf072b 'blk-mq: implement hybrid poll mode for sync O_DIRECT' (https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/06426adf072bca62ac31ea396ff2159a34f276c2). 'blk-mq: make the polling code adaptive' (https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1611.0/01838.html). Code read in the v4.10 and v5.15 trees: v5.15 block/blk-mq.c blk_mq_poll_stats_bkt (line 49), blk_poll_stats_enable / blk_mq_poll_stats_start / blk_mq_poll_stats_fn / blk_mq_poll_nsecs / blk_mq_poll_hybrid_sleep (lines 3806-3947); block/blk-sysfs.c queue_poll_delay_show/store (line 393); include/linux/blkdev.h BLK_MQ_POLL_STATS_BKTS=16 and BLK_MQ_POLL_CLASSIC=-1; block/blk-stat.c blk_stat_add / blk_rq_stat_sum. Copies are in /tmp/claude-2002/-home-jetson-src/6ac0883f-4479-466c-bec5-5fa31cffe4de/scratchpad/dl/blk-mq-v5.15.c and blk-mq-v4.10.c.
mechanisms.algorithm: The sysfs value /sys/block/<dev>/queue/io_poll_delay is stored as q->poll_nsec. Writing -1 (BLK_MQ_POLL_CLASSIC) means never sleep. Writing 0 means adaptive. Writing >0 means a fixed sleep of val*1000 ns. Default is -1, so hybrid was never on by default. Per polled request, at most once (RQF_MQ_POLL_SLEPT): nsecs = poll_nsec if it is >0, otherwise blk_mq_poll_nsecs(). That function works as follows. If poll stats are not yet enabled, it enables them and returns 0 (no sleep the first time). bucket = ddir + 2*ilog2(sectors), with 16 buckets (read/write × 8 size classes from 512 B to 64 KiB; larger requests are clamped into the last pair). If poll_stat[bucket].nr_samples is nonzero, the sleep is (mean+1)/2 ns. Stats: the sample value is now - rq->io_start_time_ns, measured from issue to completion. Samples go into per-CPU accumulators of {min, max, mean, nr_samples, batch}. A 100 ms window (blk_stat_activate_msecs(q->poll_cb, 100)) is armed on a completion when no window is active. When the timer fires it sums the per-CPU stats (dst->mean = (src->batch + dst->mean*dst->nr)/(dst->nr+src->nr)) and copies only buckets that have samples into q->poll_stat. Old values therefore persist until new samples arrive. Sleep: an hrtimer sleeper on CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE + io_schedule(). The first arm is HRTIMER_MODE_REL. After a spurious wake it is re-armed as HRTIMER_MODE_ABS on the same expiry, so the deadline does not drift. The loop breaks early if the request is already MQ_RQ_COMPLETE. The caller then busy-polls as in classic mode. Why half the mean: it is not derived. The source comment calls it 'an optimistic guess, use half of the mean service time ... We can (and should) make this smarter. For instance, if the completion latencies are tight, we can get closer than just half the mean.' Halving leaves room for variance in completion time and for the wake-up latency, both unmodelled. Axboe later said '60% of mean has also, in testing, been shown to be a win' (2017 reply, next entry).
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This only works when the waiter knows when the event was started, as with an I/O it issued itself. Our watcher does not know when a random GPU lane will post flag1, so 'sleep half the mean' does not apply to the first request of a burst. It does apply in two places where we do know the start time. (1) Inside a burst: after the watcher sets flag2, the next lane's flag1 follows after a gap g. g = (lane sees flag2) + unlock + __syncwarp + next lane's lock, request write, membar.sys, flag1 store. Measure g per bucket, bucketed by probe/helper id, the analogue of ddir and size. (2) After a probed-kernel launch: our launch hook records t_launch. Bucket the time to the first request by (kernel function, probe), the way blk-mq buckets by size. In both cases sleep k·mean(g) or (better, see next entries) min(g) - (A+C), then WFE. Break-even on this board: a sleep of n us lasts n+4 us with slack 1 us and costs about 1.2 us of CPU per wake (given measurements). Sleeping saves CPU only when g > about 5-6 us, and it saves latency only if n+4 <= g. Given requests about 9 us apart inside a warp, and the given fact that a host call is served in about 10 us, the flag2→flag1 gap is probably only a few us. I did not measure it, so check the existing timestamps. If it is under about 5 us, the in-burst regime should be spin/WFE only, and hybrid only pays for the gap from launch to the first request. Use clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME) for the same reason v5.15 switches to HRTIMER_MODE_ABS. Use a 100 ms stats window with keep-last-value semantics, and skip sleeping until the first window has samples. That costs nothing extra.
mechanisms.measured: Axboe cover letter (2016): adaptive mode (0) kept '93% of the performance at roughly 50% CPU instead of the 100% with classic polling'. HotStorage'22, Optane 900P, 4 KB randread: hybrid 8.5 us / 113,846 IOPS (1 thread) and 13.9 us / 546,968 (8 threads) vs classic 8.1 / 120,470 and 13.6 / 571,659. IISWC'19 'Faster than Flash' (Koh et al.): hybrid cut latency at most 8.2% vs interrupts, while pure polling cut it up to 33% on average. Hybrid was 5% slower than polling 'because the expected time to sleep ... is highly inaccurate', and still used 58% (sequential) and 56% (random) CPU. OSDI'21 cinterrupts Fig. 2 (Optane P4800X): with 2 processes or mixed 4K/64K sizes, hybrid used 1.5x-2.7x the CPU of interrupts with no noticeable gain.

mechanisms.name: Proposed refinements of hybrid sleep: Bates 'minimum completion time minus wake adjust', Axboe 'track A+C' (not merged)
mechanisms.where: Stephen Bates, '[PATCH] blk-mq: Improvements to the hybrid polling sleep time calculation', 2017-08-21 (https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1708.2/04129.html). Axboe reply (https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1708.2/05427.html). Bates reply (https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1708.3/03922.html).
mechanisms.algorithm: Bates added sysfs hyb_use_min (sleep = bucket min instead of mean/2, because 'polling before the minimum completion time makes no sense') and hyb_adjust (ns subtracted from the sleep to allow for OS wake time). Axboe rejected the extra knob. His alternative: model completion as A+B+C, with A = time to go to sleep, B = sleep, C = time to wake. Track A+C online and sleep for (expected completion - (A+C)). He also wanted to pass the expected sleep length down to the idle governor so it can choose a C-state. He suggested making hybrid the default and noted that 60% of the mean also tested as a win. Bates agreed that the wake time should be auto-calculated. I found no evidence the patch was merged; the v5.15 code still uses mean/2.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the best-fitting rule for our in-burst and after-launch gaps. sleep = max(0, min_or_p10(g) - (A+C)_measured), and do not sleep if that is under about 2 us. On this board (A+C) is directly observable on every wake at zero cost: oversleep = t_woken - t_deadline (vDSO clock_gettime). On an idle CPU it is about 4 us with slack 1 us (given). Track it with an EWMA. When it grows, the CPU is contended: the watcher waited on the run queue. That is a free run-queue-delay signal, and the scheduler-hint idea becomes 'raise the period when oversleep rises', the regime where the measurements say M100 wins under load. Axboe's 'tell the idle governor how long we sleep' matches the board measurements: with cpuidle off, WFE had no measurable extra power, while S10 cost +200 mW, so wake frequency, not spinning, is what costs power here. A second cheap use of the 'publish your expected sleep' idea, going the other way: the watcher writes its next-wake deadline into pinned memory, and the waiting GPU lane can __nanosleep (sm_70+, so available on Orin sm_87) until then instead of looping on membar.sys + ld.global. In the checked-out tree (/home/jetson/src/bpftime HEAD b9fee864, attach/nv_attach_impl/trampoline/default_trampoline.cu:131-171, make_helper_call) the GPU side is a tight 'membar.sys; ld.global flag2; bra' spin behind a grid-wide spin lock. GPU cost of the change: one load of the deadline; the benefit, less polling traffic on the shared DRAM fabric, is not measured.
mechanisms.measured: Bates table (Intel Optane; latency unit not labelled in the mail, presumably us): classic (-1): 8.4 at 100% CPU. Mean/2 (0): 8.4 at 57%. min, adjust 0: 10.3 at 34%. min, adjust 1000 ns: 9.9 at 37%. min, adjust 2000 ns: 8.4 at 47%. min, adjust 10000 ns: 8.4 at 100%. Text: min instead of half took CPU from 59% to 38%.

mechanisms.name: Removal of blk-mq hybrid polling (2023); io_poll_delay is now a stub
mechanisms.where: Commit 54bdd67d0f88 'blk-mq: remove hybrid polling', Keith Busch, 2023-03-20 (https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/54bdd67d0f88489ac88f7664b56cb7c93799d84d). mechanisms.algorithm: Rationale from the commit: io_uring is the only user-space path that polls completions, and it always sets BLK_POLL_NOSLEEP, which made hybrid dead code. Hellwig: 'There is no point in sleeping for the expected I/O completion timeout in the io_uring async polling model as we never poll for a specific I/O.' The sysfs knob was kept as a no-op fixed at -1. The exact mainline release tag of 54bdd67d is unverified; the 6.8 tree on this board confirms it is gone.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The removal rationale is a warning for us. Expected-completion sleeping only makes sense when you wait for one specific event with a known start. A multiplexed poller that serves many independent requesters (our watcher serving all lanes and kernels) has no single deadline, so mean/2 is wrong there. For the watcher this means sleep-before-poll applies only to known-start gaps: after flag2, and after a launch. Arrivals with random phase need either a fixed period (the square-root rule) or a spin window (Karlin).

mechanisms.name: io_uring hybrid IOPOLL (IORING_SETUP_HYBRID_IOPOLL): sleep half the running minimum
mechanisms.where: Present in v6.13 io_uring/rw.c: io_hybrid_iopoll_delay, io_uring_hybrid_poll, io_do_iopoll (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.13/io_uring/rw.c, around lines 812-830 and 1161-1243). io_uring.c sets ctx->hybrid_poll_time = LLONG_MAX at ctx creation and rejects HYBRID_IOPOLL without IOPOLL. Patch series 'io_uring: releasing CPU resources when polling', by hexue (Samsung), v8 (https://lists.openwall.net/linux-kernel/2024/08/12/48) and v9 (https://lkml.rescloud.iu.edu/2411.0/00287.html). I verified the file contents, not the merge commit hash.
mechanisms.algorithm: At issue: req->iopoll_start = ktime_get_ns() and clear REQ_F_IOPOLL_STATE. At reap: if the request has not slept yet and hybrid_poll_time != LLONG_MAX, sleep_time = hybrid_poll_time/2 ('Using half the running time to do schedule'). Then hrtimer sleeper (REL, TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE, io_schedule), set REQ_F_IOPOLL_STATE (one sleep per request), then a classic poll. After the poll, runtime = now - iopoll_start - sleep_time. If hybrid_poll_time > runtime, hybrid_poll_time = runtime. So the estimator is a running minimum over the ring's lifetime. It never increases and is never reset, which is deliberate: 'Use minimum sleep time if we're polling devices with different latencies.' The first request never sleeps, because the value starts at LLONG_MAX.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the cheapest estimator to copy for the after-flag2 gap: keep one int64 running minimum (perhaps per probe id) and sleep min/2 only if min/2 > about 5 us (board break-even: n+4 us latency, 1.2 us CPU per wake). It is O(1) with no window timer. The weakness: one fast outlier pins the sleep low forever, which wastes CPU but never adds latency. For us, add decay (for example, reset at each kernel launch, which our launch hooks already see). Signal: the flag2→flag1 gap, timestamped by the watcher with CNTVCT or clock_gettime, at zero extra cost.

mechanisms.name: io_uring SQPOLL thread: idle timeout, park, IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP handshake
mechanisms.where: Local 6.8 tree: /home/jetson/src/l4t-r39.2.1/Linux_for_Tegra/source/kernel/kernel-noble/io_uring/sqpoll.c:223-332 (io_sq_thread), :168-203 (__io_sq_thread; IORING_SQPOLL_CAP_ENTRIES_VALUE 8 at :21), :389-391 (idle default), :81-85 (max idle across rings sharing the thread). io_uring.c:3801-3802 (IORING_ENTER_SQ_WAKEUP → wake_up(&sqd->wait)). uapi io_uring.h comment at the top: the app must check NEED_WAKEUP after updating the SQ tail, with a full smp_mb(). liburing 2.7 src/queue.c sq_ring_needs_enter (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/axboe/liburing/liburing-2.7/src/queue.c).
mechanisms.algorithm: sq_thread_idle = msecs_to_jiffies(p->sq_thread_idle); if that is 0, HZ, meaning 1 s by default. On this board HZ=250, so the idle granularity is 4 ms. Loop: process all rings (submit up to 8 SQEs per ring when several rings share the thread, and reap iopoll). sqt_spin = any work done, iopoll still pending, or task_work run. If sqt_spin or now <= timeout: if sqt_spin, set timeout = jiffies + idle. If need_resched(), drop the lock and cond_resched(). Continue spinning. Otherwise park: prepare_to_wait(TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE); for each ring, atomic_or(IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP, sq_flags); smp_mb__after_atomic(); re-check io_sqring_entries(); if any, do not sleep. Otherwise schedule(). On wake, clear NEED_WAKEUP and set timeout = jiffies + idle. User side (liburing): write the SQ tail; io_uring_smp_mb(); if sq_flags & NEED_WAKEUP, call io_uring_enter(IORING_ENTER_SQ_WAKEUP), which calls wake_up(&sqd->wait). This is the Dekker store→fence→load handshake: whichever side stores second sees the other's flag, so no wake-up is lost. Note: spinning is plain cpu_relax-free looping, and the idle timer is reset by any work, so this is spin-then-block with a fixed 1 s (default) spin budget measured from the last work, not from the first.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Three parts carry over. (1) Measure the spin window from the last request (reset on every flag1), not from a fixed start. Our old policy N already does this with 200 us. SQPOLL's 1 s default is a throughput setting far above the Karlin break-even (spin budget roughly equal to the cost of one block/wake, here about 5 us of overshoot plus 1.2 us of CPU), so do not copy the constant. (2) The park handshake cannot be copied directly. The GPU has no wake primitive, so it cannot do io_uring_enter, and its only 'doorbell' is the cache-line write that WFE sees, while the scheduler still counts the WFE thread as running (the 14% load loss). (3) It can be copied for the CPU-side requester we do have, the launch hook. Park the watcher with no timer at all (futex wait) while no probed kernel is in flight. Publish a 'watcher parked' flag. Our cuLaunchKernel hook does store(inflight++); fence; if parked, futex_wake. The watcher does store(parked=1); fence; re-check inflight; then futex_wait. That is the same Dekker pattern. Idle-GPU cost drops from M100's ~10k wakes/s (about 1.2% of a core at 1.2 us/wake; +33-61 mW measured) to zero wakes. The cost moves to one futex_wake syscall on launch paths that find the watcher parked (a few us, not measured here). Risk: kernels launched in ways our hook does not see (CUDA graphs, for example) would never wake the watcher. Keep a slow backstop timer (for example 1-4 ms, one tick) while parked unless all launch paths are covered. When a kernel is in flight, the need_resched rule from entry 1 still applies.

mechanisms.name: NVMe poll queues (no interrupt vector) and the CQ phase tag
mechanisms.where: Local 6.8 tree: /home/jetson/src/l4t-r39.2.1/Linux_for_Tegra/source/kernel/kernel-noble/drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:100-102 (module param poll_queues, default 0), :2267-2291 (poll queues = min(nr_poll_queues, nr_io_queues-1), IRQ vectors only for the rest), :1158-1165 (adapter_alloc_cq sets NVME_CQ_IRQ_ENABLED only if !NVMEQ_POLLED), :989-994 (nvme_cqe_pending: (status & 1) == cq_phase), :1119-1132 (nvme_poll: cheap phase check, then take cq_poll_lock and reap the whole batch), :1053 (phase flips when the head wraps).
mechanisms.algorithm: Polled I/O (RWF_HIPRI or io_uring IOPOLL) is mapped to HCTX_TYPE_POLL queues whose completion queue is created with interrupts disabled, so nothing ever interrupts and completions are found only by polling. Other I/O goes to interrupt-driven queues. Completion detection is one lock-free load of the next CQE's phase bit compared with the expected phase (flipped on every ring wrap). The lock is taken only when work exists, and then every pending CQE is reaped in one pass and the CQ doorbell is written once.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: (a) Split host calls into two classes, as poll and IRQ queues do. Requests whose result the lane waits for (map lookup or update) take the low-latency path. Fire-and-forget requests (bpf_printk, ringbuf or perf output) can be posted to a ring without waiting for flag2 and drained on the slow periodic tick (M100 or longer). That removes them from the latency-critical spin entirely. (b) Replace the single flag1/flag2 slot behind a grid-wide spin lock (the current make_helper_call serializes all lanes of all warps) with a ring of request slots carrying a phase bit. One watcher wake then drains all posted requests. With the square-root model, wake cost c is amortised over k requests per wake (effectively c/k), so T* shrinks by sqrt(k) at the same CPU. Signal: the phase bit of the next slot, which is also exactly the cache line that WFE should monitor. Cost: GPU-side atomics to claim slots instead of a lock; CPU side unchanged.

mechanisms.name: SPDK reactor poll/interrupt mode and the dynamic scheduler
mechanisms.where: SPDK v24.09: lib/event/reactor.c (reactor_run main loop, reactor_interrupt_run = spdk_fd_group_wait(fgrp, -1), busy/idle TSC accounting in _reactor_run, scheduler gather every g_scheduler_period), module/scheduler/dynamic/scheduler_dynamic.c (g_scheduler_load_limit=20, g_scheduler_core_limit=80, g_scheduler_core_busy=95; _balance_idle, _balance_active, balance()), lib/event/app_rpc.c (default period: 'set it now to 1 second' = SPDK_SEC_TO_USEC), lib/thread/thread.c (period_poller_interrupt_init → timerfd; busy_poller_interrupt_init → eventfd; busy_poller_set_interrupt_mode writes the eventfd so it stays level-triggered), doc/scheduler.md. Fetched from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spdk/spdk/v24.09/...
mechanisms.algorithm: Each poller returns BUSY or IDLE. The reactor adds elapsed TSC to busy_tsc or idle_tsc. Every scheduler period (default 1 s once a scheduler is set; the static scheduler sets 0, meaning never) the scheduling reactor gathers per-thread and per-core deltas. busy% = busy*100/(busy+idle). A thread is active if busy% >= load_limit (20). Pass 1 moves all idle threads to the main core. Pass 2 spreads active threads so no core exceeds core_limit (80%). A core at or above core_busy (95%) counts as overloaded. Any reactor left with zero threads is switched to interrupt mode: it blocks in epoll_wait(-1) on an fd group where periodic pollers are timerfds and 'busy' pollers are eventfds. Reactors that receive threads go back to poll mode. The main core's frequency is lowered or raised by a governor (rte_power) according to busy vs idle. With --interrupt-mode at startup, everything is fd-driven from the beginning.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The SPDK rule makes the mode decision on a slow period (1 s) from a duty-cycle measurement, separate from the fast wake path. Watcher analogue: every 100 ms to 1 s, compute busy% = time spent serving / wall time from the watcher's own TSC (free), plus the request rate λ. If busy% >= 20% (at ~10 us per request that means λ >= ~20k req/s, roughly a sustained warp-burst phase), use WFE/poll mode. If below, use timed-sleep mode with the square-root period, or park (SQPOLL entry) when no kernel is in flight. Add the core_busy idea with system load: if the other cores' busy% from /proc/stat is >= 95% (6 CPU-bound threads), forbid WFE mode regardless, because the measurements show W loses 14% of load there and M100 is best. Cost: one /proc/stat read per period, tens of us at 1 Hz, which is negligible (cost not measured here). SPDK's interrupt mode itself needs an fd that the device signals (MSI-X eventfd, timerfd), and nothing on the GPU side can signal an fd mid-kernel, so only the timerfd half (periodic poll) applies to us.
mechanisms.measured: No performance numbers in the docs read. Constants: load_limit 20%, core_limit 80%, core_busy 95%, period 1 s (default via RPC).

mechanisms.name: 'When Poll is More Energy Efficient than Interrupt' (Harris & Altiparmak, HotStorage 2022)
mechanisms.where: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10410822 (DOI 10.1145/3538643.3539747). Text at /tmp/claude-2002/-home-jetson-src/6ac0883f-4479-466c-bec5-5fa31cffe4de/scratchpad/dl/stor/pollenergy.txt
mechanisms.algorithm: Measurement study, not an algorithm. Setup: Xeon E3-1230 v5 with Optane 900P, kernel 5.15.16, C-states enabled, whole-system power meter at 1 Hz, fio preadv2 with RWF_HIPRI, 1 KB-128 KB, 1-64 threads. Findings: Obs. 3, CPU utilization does not track power. Obs. 4, hybrid triggers as many context switches as interrupts, while classic triggers none. Obs. 5, hybrid pays both costs: scheduler loads/stores 786 M/s, comparable to classic's block-layer polling at 759 M/s, plus hrtimer functions at 100 M/s. Obs. 6, for low-latency requests classic polling is the most energy-efficient (bytes/J), and interrupts win for high-latency requests. Hybrid is the least energy-efficient overall.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This independently confirms our board result. WFE spinning (W) showed no measurable extra power with cpuidle off, while S10 (sleeps of ~10 us) cost +200 mW, S50 +70 mW and M100 +33-61 mW. Frequent short sleeps are a power cost, not a saving, because each wake costs scheduler and timer work (1.2 us CPU per wake on this board). Implication: on an idle CPU during a burst, WFE is both the lowest-latency and the lowest-power choice. Timed sleeps only make sense for long gaps, and W's real cost is CPU stolen from other runnable threads, which is a scheduling problem rather than an energy one. Signal for choosing: whether other threads are runnable (the need_resched analogues: oversleep, schedstat run_delay, /proc/stat busy%), not CPU% of the watcher.

mechanisms.name: Cinterrupts adaptive coalescing (Tai, Smolyar, Wei, Tsafrir, OSDI 2021): burst detection by deadline extension, plus requester semantic hints
mechanisms.where: https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi21-tai.pdf, Algorithm 1 (sec. 3.2), sec. 5.2 'Selection of ∆ and thr', Fig. 2. Text at /tmp/claude-2002/-home-jetson-src/6ac0883f-4479-466c-bec5-5fa31cffe4de/scratchpad/dl/stor/cint.txt
mechanisms.algorithm: Device side. Parameters ∆ and thr. coalesced=0; timeout=now+∆. Loop: while now<timeout, on each new completion set timeout=now+∆ (burst detection) and if ++coalesced>=thr, fire the IRQ and reset. When the quiescent interval ∆ elapses with coalesced>0, fire the IRQ and reset, then set timeout=now+∆. The result is an interrupt when a quiet gap of ∆ follows a burst, or every thr completions. Choosing ∆: from the inter-arrival distribution, as the 90th/99th percentile. Optane got ∆=6 us (p90 inter-arrival 6 us non-batched, 1 us batched). P3700 got ∆=15 us (p99 15 us). thr is the smallest value where throughput plateaus, 16-32, so thr=32. The full cinterrupts design adds requester-supplied bits in the NVMe command: Urgent (interrupt immediately) and Barrier (marks the last request of a batch, so interrupt when it completes), because device-side heuristics 'will always fall short due to a semantic gap'.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the burst rule, distinct from the idle rule. Replace N's fixed 200 us hot window with a deadline extended by ∆ on every served request. ∆ = p90-p99 of the in-burst inter-request spacing, measured online (about 9 us given, so ∆ ≈ 15-20 us). Add a cap analogous to thr: at most ~32 requests or ~1 tick of continuous hot time, then re-check the contention signal, so a long burst cannot monopolise a core under load. The semantic-hint half is the strongest idea for us and costs almost nothing. In make_helper_call, the lane knows __activemask() and its lane id, so it can write 'more_coming = popc(activemask >> (lane+1))' (or a Barrier bit on the last active lane) into the request. The watcher then stays in WFE exactly while more lanes are pending and sleeps or parks immediately after the Barrier, with no ∆ tail of wasted spin. Kernel exit (the CUDA event seen by launch tracking) is a coarser Barrier. GPU cost: one popc and one extra store per request. CPU cost: zero. Limitation: other warps and blocks may post right after this warp's Barrier, so keep a short ∆ after it rather than zero.
mechanisms.measured: Fig. 2 (Optane P4800X, one core): hybrid polling matches polling for one thread of uniform requests. With 2 processes, or 4K plus 64K, it uses 1.5x-2.7x more CPU than interrupts with no noticeable gain. Sec. 5.3: cinterrupts matched default sync latency with up to 35% more async throughput, and matched the adaptive strategy's throughput with up to 37% lower latency.

notes:
The common rule across the whole family, and how it applies to this board: block only when the expected gap is larger than the full sleep round trip, and sleep for (gap estimate) - (A+C), where A+C is the cost of going to sleep plus waking. FAST'12 measured that round trip as 1.4 us (Tb). On this board the given measurements put it at about 4 us of overshoot (a sleep of n us lasts n+4 us with timer slack 1 us) plus about 1.2 us of CPU per wake, so about 5-6 us. Consequences:
(1) Inside a warp burst (requests about 9 us apart, served in about 10 us), the flag2→next-flag1 gap is probably below that, so the burst regime is spin/WFE only. Hybrid sleeping in the blk-mq / io_uring HYBRID_IOPOLL style pays only for the gap from launch to the first request, and for any flag2→flag1 gap whose running minimum or p10 is above ~6 us. Measure that gap from existing timestamps; it is not measured here.
(2) 'Why half the mean' has no derivation. The source calls it an optimistic guess. Bates showed half polls before the minimum, and minimum-based sleeping cut CPU from 59% to 38%. Axboe said 60% also wins and proposed tracking A+C. io_uring's 6.13 hybrid uses half of a running minimum.
(3) Sleeping on an expected completion time requires a known start. The block maintainers removed hybrid polling in 2023 because the multiplexed io_uring poller has no single deadline, and our watcher is in the same position for the first request of a burst.
(4) The kernel pollers are cheap under load only because they exit on need_resched(). The user-space stand-ins available here are oversleep (free, vDSO clock), field 2 of /proc/thread-self/schedstat (SCHED_INFO=y on this kernel), and getrusage ru_nivcsw. PSI is not available (CONFIG_PSI not set). The kernel is HZ=250 and full PREEMPT.
(5) Energy: HotStorage'22 found classic polling the most energy-efficient and hybrid the least, which matches W at about 0 mW vs S10 at +200 mW. Wake frequency costs power; WFE spinning does not. W's real cost is CPU taken from other runnable threads.

Suggested composite policy, built only from mechanisms above:
- No probed kernel in flight: park on a futex, with the launch hook waking it via the SQPOLL NEED_WAKEUP Dekker handshake, plus a 1-4 ms backstop if graph launches are not hooked.
- Kernel in flight: WFE, with the hot deadline extended by ∆ ≈ p90-p99 of the in-burst spacing (cinterrupts), ended early by a GPU 'more_coming / Barrier' hint, and capped at ~32 requests or 1 tick.
- After the burst: timed sleeps at the square-root period with clock_nanosleep TIMER_ABSTIME.
- Every 100 ms to 1 s (SPDK style): if busy% < 20% or system busy >= 95% or oversleep/run_delay is rising, forbid WFE and use M100.
- Structural: a phase-bit ring (NVMe CQ style) instead of the grid-wide lock with a single slot, so one wake drains k requests (c/k in the square-root model), and fire-and-forget helpers such as printk or ringbuf output go to a lazily drained ring.
- GPU side: __nanosleep until a watcher-published deadline instead of the tight membar.sys/ld loop seen in default_trampoline.cu:131-171 of /home/jetson/src/bpftime HEAD b9fee864. The dev branch may differ; I did not check it.

mechanisms.name: glibc PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP (EWMA spin budget)
mechanisms.where: glibc-2.39 (the Ubuntu 2.39-0ubuntu8.8 on this board) nptl/pthread_mutex_lock.c lines 134-166; sysdeps/nptl/pthreadP.h max_adaptive_count(); sysdeps/generic/adaptive_spin_count.h DEFAULT_ADAPTIVE_COUNT; sysdeps/nptl/dl-tunables.list glibc.pthread.mutex_spin_count; sysdeps/nptl/pthread_mutex_backoff.h (used on aarch64) vs sysdeps/x86_64/nptl/pthread_mutex_backoff.h; include/atomic.h atomic_spin_nop
mechanisms.algorithm: On a failed trylock: max_cnt = MIN(max_adaptive_count(), __spins*2 + 10), where max_adaptive_count() = tunable glibc.pthread.mutex_spin_count (INT_32, min 0, max 32767, default 100 = DEFAULT_ADAPTIVE_COUNT). Loop: spin_count = exp_backoff + (jitter & (exp_backoff-1)); cnt += spin_count; if cnt >= max_cnt -> LLL_MUTEX_LOCK (futex block) and stop; else run atomic_spin_nop() spin_count times; exp_backoff = get_next_backoff(exp_backoff); continue while lock word != 0 or trylock fails. After acquiring (either way): __spins += (cnt - __spins)/8 (EWMA, gain 1/8, integer division, stored per mutex as a short). Units are loop iterations, not time. x86_64 only: jitter from get_fast_jitter() and binary exponential backoff capped at MAX_BACKOFF=16. aarch64 uses the generic header: get_jitter() returns 0 and get_next_backoff() returns 1, so every iteration is spin_count=1; sysdeps/aarch64/atomic-machine.h defines no atomic_spin_nop, so it is the empty no-op from include/atomic.h. Net on this Orin: a tight loop of plain load + trylock, no YIELD/ISB/WFE hint, at most min(100, 2*__spins+10) iterations (well under 1 us), then futex wait.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Mapping: one 'wait' = one gap between host-call requests; 'cnt' = how long the watcher stayed hot before the next request came (capped by the window). Rule to copy: hot_window_next = min(CAP, 2*ewma_gap + base), ewma_gap += (observed_gap_capped - ewma_gap)/8, applied after each request. Signal: time since last request (CLOCK_MONOTONIC on each served request, ~25 ns via vDSO). Unlike glibc, the budget has to be time-based (us), and CAP should be set by the cost model (see Lim-Agarwal / Karlin) rather than 100 iterations. Cost on this board: one clock read + a few integer ops per request, negligible next to ~10 us service time. Limit: an EWMA with gain 1/8 tracks the mean only, so a bimodal gap distribution (9 us inside a warp burst vs ms between kernel launches) gives a window that fits neither mode; with 2x+10 it sizes to the mean of the mixture. Use it per mode (inside-burst vs between-launch) or use KVM-style grow/shrink instead.

mechanisms.name: Linux mutex optimistic spinning (spin only while owner is on a CPU; MCS/OSQ queue; WFE wait on arm64)
mechanisms.where: Linux 6.8.12 (local tree /home/jetson/src/l4t-r39.2.1/Linux_for_Tegra/source/kernel/kernel-noble, same file as upstream v6.8) kernel/locking/mutex.c mutex_can_spin_on_owner() 392-415, mutex_spin_on_owner() 352-386, mutex_optimistic_spin() 441-510, first-waiter re-spin at 696-700; kernel/locking/osq_lock.c 146-147; arch/arm64/include/asm/barrier.h smp_cond_load_relaxed 193-204; arch/arm64/include/asm/cmpxchg.h __CMPWAIT_CASE 211-227; arch/arm64/include/asm/vdso/processor.h cpu_relax() = 'yield'; running config: CONFIG_MUTEX_SPIN_ON_OWNER=y, CONFIG_PREEMPT=y, HZ=250
mechanisms.algorithm: Entry gate mutex_can_spin_on_owner(): return 0 if need_resched(); owner = lock owner; if owner != NULL return owner_on_cpu(owner) (owner->on_cpu && !vcpu_is_preempted(task_cpu(owner))); owner NULL -> spin (lock is being released). Then take the OSQ (per-lock MCS queue so only one task spins on the owner field). Spin loop mutex_spin_on_owner(): while lock->owner == owner { barrier(); if (!owner_on_cpu(owner) || need_resched()) return false; cpu_relax(); } i.e. no time or count limit at all: the spin length is fully determined by the owner's running state and by whether anyone else wants this CPU. After owner changes: trylock; on failure loop again. Preemption is disabled while spinning. If it falls out because of need_resched(), it calls schedule_preempt_disabled() and then blocks. A waiter that becomes first in the wait list (first==true) spins again via mutex_optimistic_spin(lock, ww_ctx, &waiter) after each wakeup. OSQ waiters wait with smp_cond_load_relaxed(&node->locked, VAL || need_resched() || vcpu_is_preempted(prev cpu)); on arm64 that is: VAL=READ_ONCE; if cond break; __cmpwait: 'sevl; wfe; ldxr tmp,[ptr]; eor tmp,tmp,val; cbnz tmp,1f; wfe; 1:'. The source comment: need_resched() arrives with an IPI, which wakes the monitor-wait (WFE). So the kernel's own spin-then-block on arm64 = WFE on the cache line + bail out on need_resched().
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the closest model for policy W, and it explains W's 14% loss: the kernel spins only while the owner is on a CPU AND need_resched() is false; W only had the first check. Mapping: owner_on_cpu(owner) <-> 'a probed kernel is in flight' (launch-hook CUDA events, checked every ~100 us on the evtstrm wake; cudaEventQuery cost per check already paid in W). need_resched() <-> 'another runnable task wants my CPU'. Userspace has no need_resched flag and no IPI into a WFE, but the evtstrm wakes the WFE every ~100 us (ARCH_TIMER_EVT_STREAM_PERIOD_US=100 in include/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.h), so on each wake read a preemption signal: (a) getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD).ru_nivcsw delta (involuntary context switches; one syscall, estimated ~1 us, not measured), or (b) /proc/thread-self/schedstat field 2 (run_delay ns; CONFIG_SCHED_INFO=y and CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS=y here, file readable; open+read estimated a few us, not measured; keep the fd open and pread). If nivcsw rose or run_delay grew since the last check, stop WFE and fall back to M100 sleeping (the kernel's 'need_resched -> schedule()'), and mark the episode non-spinnable for some time (see rwsem NONSPINNABLE). With CONFIG_PREEMPT=y and HZ=250, the tick preemption of a CPU-bound W thread is what produces the 13-31% calls >1 ms; checking every 100 us bounds the time the watcher competes after it has been preempted once, it cannot prevent the first preemption. CONFIG_PSI is not set on this kernel, so /proc/pressure/cpu is not available as a system-wide signal.
mechanisms.measured: No numbers in source.

mechanisms.name: Linux rwsem reader-owned spin with a time cap, NONSPINNABLE latch, and rtmutex top-waiter spin
mechanisms.where: local 6.8.12 kernel/locking/rwsem.c rwsem_rspin_threshold() 806-817, rwsem_optimistic_spin() 819-935, RWSEM_WAIT_TIMEOUT 359; kernel/locking/rtmutex.c rtmutex_spin_on_owner() 1476-1511; CONFIG_RWSEM_SPIN_ON_OWNER=y
mechanisms.algorithm: Writer spinning on a writer-owned rwsem: same owner-on-cpu rule as mutex (no time limit). When readers own it (owner unknown, so on-CPU cannot be checked) spinning gets a time budget: threshold = sched_clock() + (20 + readers)*NSEC_PER_USEC/2, readers capped at 30, i.e. (10 + nr_readers/2) us, max 25 us; reset whenever the owner state changes from non-reader to reader; sched_clock() is checked only once every 16 iterations (!(++loop & 0xf)) to keep the poll loop cheap; on expiry rwsem_set_nonspinnable(sem) sets a flag in the owner word so later spinners skip spinning until a new writer takes the lock. Non-writer state also checks need_resched() each iteration, and an RT task stops if the previous owner state was not WRITER. Handoff: a waiter that has waited RWSEM_WAIT_TIMEOUT = DIV_ROUND_UP(HZ,250) jiffies (= 1 jiffy = 4 ms at HZ=250) may set the handoff bit. rtmutex (PI futexes go through it): spin while owner unchanged and owner_on_cpu(owner) and !need_resched() and current is still the top waiter; cpu_relax() between checks.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Two ideas carry over. (1) When 'owner state' is unknown, use a short fixed time budget instead of spinning unboundedly: for the watcher, when no launch tracking is available (e.g. a probed kernel started on a stream we did not hook), allow WFE for only a short window after the last request, then sleep. (2) The NONSPINNABLE latch: once the watcher sees itself preempted (nivcsw / run_delay rose), set a 'no-WFE' flag that stays set until an event that predicts low CPU contention (e.g. the next kernel launch hook, or N consecutive M100 periods with run_delay delta ~0). This gives hysteresis and avoids flapping between W and sleep under full load. (3) Check the clock only every 16th iteration: on this board a CNTVCT read is cheap, but the general rule (do not put syscalls or /proc reads on every iteration) holds; with WFE the natural check rate is the 100 us evtstrm. rtmutex's 'stop if no longer top waiter' has no direct counterpart (there is one watcher).
mechanisms.measured: No numbers in source; the 10 + n/2 us formula is described in the source comment as 'just a heuristic and is subjected to change'.

mechanisms.name: KVM halt-polling (adaptive poll window grown/shrunk from observed halt length)
mechanisms.where: local 6.8.12 virt/kvm/kvm_main.c halt_poll_ns_grow=2 (l.85), halt_poll_ns_grow_start=10000 (l.90), halt_poll_ns_shrink=0 (l.95), grow_halt_poll_ns() 3718-3735, shrink_halt_poll_ns() 3737-3754, kvm_vcpu_halt() ~3860-3930; arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_host.h KVM_HALT_POLL_NS_DEFAULT 500000 (x86: 200000)
mechanisms.algorithm: Per vCPU state halt_poll_ns (starts 0), clamped to max_halt_poll_ns (module param halt_poll_ns, default 500000 ns on arm64). On halt: if halt_poll_ns>0, poll kvm_vcpu_check_block() with cpu_relax() until ktime > start+halt_poll_ns; if no event, block (schedule). Afterwards halt_ns = total halted time (poll + block). Update: if wakeup invalid -> shrink; else if halt_ns <= halt_poll_ns -> keep; else if halt_poll_ns>0 && halt_ns > max -> shrink (long block, polling wasted); else if halt_poll_ns < max && halt_ns < max -> grow (short halt that the window just missed). grow: val *= grow (2); if val < grow_start (10 us) val = grow_start. shrink: shrink==0 (default) -> val = 0, else val /= shrink; if val < grow_start -> 0. Polling counts as successful if the vCPU was never scheduled out, even if the event came after the poll loop ended.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the closest structural analog to the watcher: it polls for an asynchronous arrival (an interrupt) rather than a lock release, and sizes the poll window from the observed gap. Direct port: hot_ns starts 0; after each served request measure gap = time to next request; if gap <= hot_ns keep; if gap > MAX (e.g. MAX = 1 ms or the period cap of the sleep phase) shrink (to 0 by default, or /2); if hot_ns < gap < MAX grow: hot_ns = max(2*hot_ns, 10 us). The hot phase is WFE (cheap, ~2 us wake) and the block phase is the M100/S-period sleeping. Signals: time since last request; optionally 'kernel in flight' from launch events to cap the window at kernel end. Warp bursts (~9 us between lanes) keep the window open via 'gap <= hot_ns'; the between-launch gap decides grow/shrink. Cost: one clock read per request plus the WFE time itself, which costs the 14% load loss only when CPUs are saturated, so combine with the preemption/idle-CPU gates (Linux mutex, Go canSpin). The default shrink-to-0 makes it reset fast after one long gap, which suits entry/exit probe patterns (requests cluster at kernel start/end).
mechanisms.measured: No numbers in source.

mechanisms.name: Go sync.Mutex (spin conditions, starvation mode)
mechanisms.where: Go 1.22 local source /usr/share/go-1.22/src/sync/mutex.go Lock/lockSlow 120-200 (starvationThresholdNs = 1e6 l.75); runtime/proc.go sync_runtime_canSpin 7045-7058, sync_runtime_doSpin 7062-7064; runtime/lock_futex.go active_spin=4, active_spin_cnt=30, passive_spin=1; runtime/asm_arm64.s procyield 916-922
mechanisms.algorithm: Spin only if: mutex locked and not starving, and runtime_canSpin(iter): iter < active_spin (4) AND ncpu > 1 AND gomaxprocs > npidle + nmspinning + 1 (at least one other P is running and not all Ps are idle/spinning) AND the local P run queue is empty. Each spin = procyield(30) = 30 x arm64 'YIELD' instruction. While spinning, set mutexWoken so Unlock does not wake a sleeper. Then block on a semaphore (runtime_SemacquireMutex, LIFO if it waited before). After wakeup, starving = waited > 1 ms (starvationThresholdNs = 1e6 ns); a starving waiter switches the mutex to starvation mode: Unlock hands ownership directly to the queue head, new arrivals do not spin or grab; exit starvation when the waiter is the last one or waited < 1 ms. Spin is a fixed small budget (4 x 30 YIELDs), not adaptive; adaptivity comes from the admission check on scheduler state.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The admission condition is the part that addresses the 14% finding directly: Go spins only if some other P is running and the run queue is empty, i.e. only when spinning does not take a CPU someone else needs. Watcher version: allow WFE only if the number of runnable tasks < number of online CPUs. Signal: /proc/loadavg field 4 numerator (currently runnable entities) or /proc/stat 'procs_running', read at the 100 us evtstrm check (cost: open/read of a small procfs file, estimated a few us to tens of us for /proc/stat, not measured; /proc/loadavg is smaller). Caveat: these are system-wide instantaneous counts and include the watcher itself, so the rule is runnable_others < ncpu (6). The 1 ms starvation threshold maps to an SLO for host calls: if a call has waited > 1 ms (detectable from the request timestamp the GPU can write, globaltimer), switch to the higher-cost mode (WFE or short sleep) for a while regardless of the CPU-cost rule. Cost on this board: YIELD on Cortex-A78AE (no SMT) is a hint with no known effect (unverified), so 4x30 YIELD is ~120 instructions; irrelevant at our timescales.
mechanisms.measured: No numbers in source.

mechanisms.name: Go runtime lock2 (futex lock: active spin, sched_yield, futex sleep) and sysmon adaptive poll period
mechanisms.where: Go 1.22 runtime/lock_futex.go lock2() ~60-115; runtime/proc.go sysmon() 5946-6080
mechanisms.algorithm: lock2: speculative Xchg; if ncpu>1 spin = active_spin (4) rounds, each: while key == unlocked try CAS, then procyield(30); then passive_spin (1) round with osyield() (sched_yield); then Xchg key=MUTEX_SLEEPING and futexsleep(-1); repeat from the top after wakeup. sysmon (Go's own periodic poller thread): idle counter = consecutive cycles in which it did no work; delay = 20 us when idle == 0; after idle > 50 (about 1 ms of 20 us sleeps) delay doubles each cycle, capped at 10 ms; usleep(delay). idle resets to 0 when retake() took a P (it did useful work); when all Ps are idle it parks on a note (notetsleep) up to forcegcperiod/2 and resets idle only if woken by a syscall exit, not on timer wakeups ('a bet that ... it may need to do it again shortly').
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: sysmon is the same shape as the watcher's old policy N (hot then doubling sleep), with constants: 20 us base, 50 idle cycles before backoff, x2, 10 ms cap, reset on useful work. Compared to N (200 us hot, 50 us doubling to 1 ms) it starts lower, stays at the short period for a counted number of empty polls rather than a time, and parks entirely when nothing can need it (all Ps idle) <-> watcher: when no probed kernel is in flight (launch tracking), park on a futex/condvar woken by the launch hook instead of polling (M100 already sleeps; this removes even the 100 us polls when the GPU is idle). Note (inference, not checked): Go's usleep on Linux goes through nanosleep and inherits the default 50 us timer slack, so its 20 us sleeps would last ~70 us; the watcher's timer slack 1 us result shows why to set PR_SET_TIMERSLACK. The yield step (osyield) is not useful for the watcher: with CPU-bound threads on all cores sched_yield under EEVDF does not guarantee the watcher gets CPU back soon.

mechanisms.name: HotSpot ObjectMonitor adaptive spin-then-block (try_spin, _SpinDuration)
mechanisms.where: openjdk/jdk master src/hotspot/share/runtime/objectMonitor.cpp at commit 2831850 (2026-09-16), comment block and code ~2184-2430; aarch64 SpinPause: src/hotspot/os_cpu/linux_aarch64/os_linux_aarch64.cpp SpinPause() and src/hotspot/cpu/aarch64/globals_aarch64.hpp OnSpinWaitInst (default 'yield', choices none/nop/isb/yield/sb/wfet), OnSpinWaitInstCount=1, OnSpinWaitDelay=40 ns (wfet only); vm_version_aarch64.cpp sets isb x2 on some CPUs (e.g. Ampere)
mechanisms.algorithm: Per-monitor _SpinDuration D, initialized to Knob_SpinLimit = 5000 ('derived by an external tool'). Constants: Knob_Bonus=100, Knob_Penalty=200, Knob_Poverty=1000, Knob_PreSpin=10, Knob_FixedSpin=0. try_spin: (1) always do a short fixed pre-spin of 10 try_lock attempts with SpinPause() so that D==0 is not absorbing; success there -> adjust_up. (2) ctr = D; if <= 0 return false (block). Loop while --ctr >= 0: every 256 iterations check for a pending safepoint and break; TATAS probe owner; if free and CAS wins -> adjust_up(D) and return true; if CAS fails -> break (no penalty); if owner changed from one non-null owner to another -> break (no penalty). (3) If ctr ran out (ctr < 0) -> adjust_down(D). adjust_up(x): if x < 5000 { if x < 1000 x = 1000; return x + 100 } else unchanged. adjust_down(x): x -= 200, floor 0. Spin frequency is fixed at 100% and duration adapts by success rate; the comment says the gain is deliberately biased toward not spinning (penalty 2x bonus), D is capped at about a round-trip context switch, and oscillation at the profitability boundary is accepted without hysteresis.
