mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Additive-increase/additive-decrease on success/failure is simple and robust to bimodal gaps: per request, if the next request arrived while hot -> window += bonus (with floor 'poverty'), else window -= penalty. Use a 2:1 penalty:bonus like HotSpot to bias toward sleeping, which matches the CPU-cost finding (more CPU -> more scheduler delay under load). The 'always pre-spin a little' rule maps to: always keep a minimal WFE window (e.g. 10-20 us, about two warp-lane gaps of ~9 us) after each request, so that the window can grow back after a quiet period. The safepoint-every-256 check maps to checking the stop flag / preemption signal at each evtstrm wake. Signal: next-request-arrived-within-window (boolean per request). Cost: negligible bookkeeping. The aarch64 spin hint menu shows WFET (WFE with timeout, FEAT_WFxT) is the modern choice, but /proc/cpuinfo on this Orin (CPU part 0xd42, Cortex-A78AE) lists no 'wfxt', so only plain WFE + evtstrm is available here.

mechanisms.name: Rust parking_lot SpinWait and eventual fairness

mechanisms.name: Karlin-Manasse-McGeoch-Owicki competitive spin-block (deterministic 2-competitive, randomized e/(e-1))
mechanisms.where: A. Karlin, M. Manasse, L. McGeoch, S. Owicki, 'Competitive randomized algorithms for non-uniform problems', SODA 1990 pp.301-309 (Algorithmica 11(6):542-571, 1994); read the SODA version at https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.896/spring04/class/www/handouts/papers/karlin.pdf, Section 3 'Spin-Block', p.306, Theorems 6-8
mechanisms.algorithm: Costs: spinning costs time spent; blocking costs C (context switch). Deterministic: spin for exactly C then block -> cost <= 2x offline optimum; Theorem 6: no deterministic algorithm is c-competitive for c < 2 against a strong adversary. Theorem 7 (randomized, weak/oblivious adversary): choose spin time t from density pi(t) = e^{t/C} / ((e-1) C) for 0 <= t <= C, 0 otherwise (increasing density: longer spins more likely); expected cost <= e/(e-1) ~= 1.58 x optimum. Theorem 8 (adaptive): A* = deterministic algorithm minimizing expected cost under a time-invariant distribution P of waits; E C_A*(sigma(P)) <= e/(e-1) E C_opt; using sample statistics to estimate P converges to that. Practical last-wait variant: if the last hold time tau < C spin for C, else block immediately; 3-competitive against a strong adversary. alpha variant (0 < alpha <= 1): if tau < alpha C spin alpha C, else block; trades competitiveness for a bound relative to always-block.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Translation for an arrival-poller: C = cost of being in 'blocked' mode for one gap = CPU cost of a sleep/wake (~1.2 us per wake-up, measured) plus the latency penalty alpha_lat x (expected extra wait to notice a request when sleeping: ~period/2 + 4 us + run-queue delay). Spin cost per us = CPU taken from others (0 if an idle core exists, about 1 core-us per us when all 6 cores are busy) plus power (not measurable with cpuidle off). The deterministic rule then says: after a request keep WFE for a time equal to C (in us-equivalents), then sleep; the randomized rule says draw that hot window from pi(t) = e^{t/C}/((e-1)C) on [0,C] (inverse CDF: t = C ln(1 + u(e-1)), u uniform in [0,1)). The last-gap rule (gap_last < C -> hot for C, else sleep at once) is a one-variable version suited to entry/exit probes. Signal: time since last request; C estimated from the watcher's measured wake cost and its run_delay (schedstat) under current load, so C grows under load -> shorter WFE windows exactly when spinning hurts.
mechanisms.measured: Theoretical bounds only: 2 (deterministic), e/(e-1) ~= 1.58 (randomized / adaptive with known distribution), 3 (last-wait rule vs strong adversary).

mechanisms.name: Karlin-Li-Manasse-Owicki empirical study: optimal-online, last-three-samples, random-walk spin thresholds
mechanisms.where: A. Karlin, K. Li, M. Manasse, S. Owicki, 'Empirical Studies of Competitive Spinning for Shared-Memory Multiprocessors', Princeton CS-TR-319-91 (March 1991), https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/1991/319.pdf, Sections 2.4-2.5 (pp.5-9), Tables 1-4 (pp.14-17); published at SOSP 1991, SIGOPS OSR 25(5):41-55 (camera-ready not read)
mechanisms.algorithm: Fixed-spin: SpinThreshold = C or C/2 (C = context switch in spins; competitive ratio 2 and 3). Optimal online for known distribution D_L per lock: choose k minimizing sum_{i<=k} i D_L[i] + (k + C) sum_{i>k} D_L[i] (continuous form: minimize int_0^tau t dP + (tau + C) int_tau^inf dP). Variable-spin framework: after each acquisition, spinsWaited = spins done + (time blocked until release) x SpinsPerSecond (the blocked part is reconstructed from the release timestamp the releaser stores); SpinThreshold := Adjust(SpinThreshold, spinsWaited). Optimal-online approximation: keep the histogram (coarse buckets) and recompute k. Last-three-samples: same minimization with D_L = average of three point masses at the last three waits tau1..tau3. Random walk: if spinsWaited > C then SpinThreshold -= 1 unit (while > 0) else += 1 unit, capped at C; implementation used units of 16 spins. Implementation details: C ~= 200 spins ~= 200 us on the Firefly; waits recorded in units of 16 spins, capped at 1008 spins; opt-approx rounded to 64-spin buckets, last-three to 16.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Gives three ready Adjust() rules for the hot-window length, all fed by the gap to the next request (the watcher knows it exactly, no reconstruction needed): (a) histogram of recent gaps (e.g. 16 us buckets up to ~1 ms) and pick the window k minimizing sum_{g<=k} g p(g) + (k + C) P(g > k) - recompute every N requests; (b) last-three gaps; (c) random walk +-16 us capped at C. Bursty warp lanes (~9 us apart) favour (a) or (b) because the distribution is bimodal; random walk is the cheapest and was nearly as good. The paper also states the conditions under which the trade-off exists at all: (a) other threads waiting for a processor and (b) the event source is running; if no other thread needs the CPU, spinning is best (Regsim: always-spin +21.5%), if work is queued spinning can lose to blocking (Hanoi: always-spin -24.4%) - same split as W idle vs W under full load.
mechanisms.measured: Table 1 (cost / offline optimum): always-block 1.58-7.24, always-spin 1.30-3.54, fixed C/2 1.27-1.50, fixed C 1.23-1.76, opt-online 1.08-1.24, last-3 1.18-1.39, random-walk 1.09-1.69; all competitive methods < 1.8. Table 2: when spinning is optimal, average spin 22-67 us vs C = 200 us; blocking optimal in 3.2-47% of waits. Elapsed time vs always-block: Regsim fixed-spin 100/200 +13.5%/+24.0%, opt-known +25.1%, opt-approx +22.3%, last-3 +23.9%, random-walk +24.7%, always-spin +21.5%; Hanoi fixed 100/200 +11.9%/+15.0%, opt-known +37.0%, opt-approx +30.1%, last-3 +30.5%, random-walk +32.1%, always-spin -24.4%.

mechanisms.name: Lim-Agarwal static two-phase waiting (Lpoll as a fixed fraction of block cost)
mechanisms.where: B.-H. Lim, A. Agarwal, 'Waiting Algorithms for Synchronization in Large-Scale Multiprocessors', MIT LCS TR-498 (1991), https://ftp.mirrorservice.org/sites/www.bitsavers.org/pdf/mit/lcs/tr/MIT-LCS-TR-0498.pdf, abstract and Section 4 (Theorems 3-4, pp.~13-15); journal version ACM TOCS 1993 (not read)
mechanisms.algorithm: Two-phase: poll until polling cost reaches Lpoll, then block (fixed extra cost B). Lpoll is expressed as alpha x B. Exponentially distributed waits (rate lambda): alpha = ln(e-1) ~= 0.54 gives cost <= e/(e-1) ~= 1.58 x offline optimum against a restricted adversary (distribution family fixed, parameter adversarial), and no dynamic algorithm does better against that adversary (Theorem 3). If lambda is known: lambda < 1/(beta B) -> block immediately (alpha=0), otherwise always poll (beta = polling cost factor; beta=1 for spinning). Uniform waits on [0,U]: alpha = (sqrt5 - 1)/2 ~= 0.618 gives <= golden ratio 1.618 (Theorem 4); with U known: U > 2 beta B -> block, else poll, worst case 4/3. Their experiments: always-block is usually close to the best; static alpha based on synchronization type does better. They prefer static L because dynamic estimation overhead can rival B with lightweight threads.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The most directly usable sizing rule for the post-request hot window. If inter-request gaps (between bursts) are roughly exponential with rate lambda (measure lambda from request timestamps over, say, the last 100 ms), and B = cost of the 'blocked' mode for one gap (wake CPU + latency penalty, see Karlin entry), then: WFE window = 0.54 B, or use the threshold rule: lambda*B > 1 -> stay in WFE for the kernel's duration, lambda*B < 1 -> sleep (M100 / S50) and skip the hot window. Within a warp burst the gaps are near-deterministic (~9 us), so keep a small fixed window covering one lane gap (>= ~10-20 us) independent of this rule. This complements the square-root period model (which picks the sleep period inside the blocked phase); Lim-Agarwal picks when to enter that phase. Signal: request rate (EWMA of inter-burst gaps), B from measured wake cost plus schedstat run_delay. Cost: counter + clock read per request.
mechanisms.measured: Bounds 1.58 (exponential, alpha=0.54) and 1.618 (uniform, alpha=0.62); empirical results on the Alewife simulator only (numbers not extracted).

mechanisms.name: Ousterhout two-phase waiting (Medusa 'pause time')
mechanisms.where: J. Ousterhout, 'Scheduling Techniques for Concurrent Systems', Proc. 3rd ICDCS, 1982 - primary text NOT read (not found online); described in Karlin-Li-Manasse-Owicki CS-TR-319-91 p.19 (Related work)
mechanisms.algorithm: As cited by Karlin et al.: blocking should be avoided when the lock will be available in less than a context switch; Medusa delayed blocking a thread for a fixed time determined by the user (two-phase waiting: spin for a fixed 'pause time', then block). Exact constants and the rule Ousterhout recommended for choosing the pause time are unverified here.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The old policy N (hot 200 us, then sleep) is exactly this form with a user-chosen pause time; the later entries in this family (Karlin/Lim-Agarwal/KVM/HotSpot) are ways to choose the pause time from observed gaps instead of a constant.
mechanisms.measured: Unverified (secondary source only).

mechanisms.name: CUDA context scheduling flags (CUDA's own spin/yield/block choice for host waits)
mechanisms.where: local /usr/local/cuda/include/cuda.h CU_CTX_SCHED_* (l.382-385) and doc comment ~6136-6160; /usr/local/cuda/include/cuda_runtime_api.h ~1738-1745 (cudaDeviceScheduleAuto)
mechanisms.algorithm: CU_CTX_SCHED_SPIN=0x01 (spin while waiting for the GPU), YIELD=0x02 (yield the thread while waiting), BLOCKING_SYNC=0x04 (block on a sync primitive), AUTO=0x00: if active CUDA contexts in the process C > logical processors P, yield; otherwise spin. 'Additionally, on Tegra devices, cudaDeviceScheduleAuto uses a heuristic based on the power profile of the platform and may choose cudaDeviceScheduleBlockingSync for low-powered devices.' (header text). On this Orin, Auto was observed to behave as blocking sync (given context). The flag in effect can be read with cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState(dev, &flags, &active).
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Use the application's chosen sync policy as a hint about the user's latency/CPU preference: if the context is SCHED_SPIN (the app already burns a core waiting on the GPU), WFE during kernels costs the same kind of CPU the app accepted, so policy W is consistent; if BLOCKING_SYNC/AUTO-on-Tegra (power-oriented), default to the sleep policy (M100 / adaptive window). One call at attach/launch time; cost negligible. Also: the app thread blocked in cudaDeviceSynchronize/cudaStreamSynchronize under BLOCKING_SYNC is not runnable, so it does not compete with the watcher; under SPIN it does (another reason to gate WFE on runnable count).
mechanisms.measured: No numbers in source.

notes:
How these systems choose spin length from observed waits (cross-cutting):
- glibc adaptive: EWMA of spins, gain 1/8; budget = min(tunable 100, 2*EWMA + 10) iterations; aarch64 build has no pause hint, no backoff, no jitter.
- Linux mutex/rtmutex: no length at all - spin while owner on CPU and !need_resched(); rwsem reader case: (10 + readers/2) us capped 25 us, then NONSPINNABLE latch.
- KVM halt-poll: window x2 (floor 10 us) when the halt was longer than the window but shorter than max (500 us arm64), reset to 0 when longer than max. haltpoll governor: x2 (floor 50 us, cap 200 us) / divide by 2.
- HotSpot: +100 on success (floor 1000), -200 on timeout, cap 5000, always pre-spin 10; biased against spinning.
- Go: fixed 4 x 30 YIELD, admission only if another P runs and runq empty; starvation switch at 1 ms wait. sysmon: 20 us, after 50 idle cycles x2 up to 10 ms, reset on work.
- parking_lot: 3 busy bursts (2/4/8 in 0.9.12, 1/2/4 in master) + 7 sched_yield, then park; spin only if nobody parked.
- Karlin TR: optimal-online over a histogram, last-3 samples, random walk +-16 spins capped at C; KMMO: spin C (2-competitive), random spin from e^{t/C}/((e-1)C) on [0,C] (1.58).
- Lim-Agarwal: static Lpoll = 0.54 B (exponential), 0.62 B (uniform); block outright if lambda < 1/B.

Mismatch to keep in mind: all lock algorithms wait for one known release whose owner is visible; the watcher waits for unknown arrivals. Translation used above: C/B (block cost) <-> CPU per wake-up (~1.2 us) + latency penalty while sleeping (period/2 + ~4 us + run-queue delay); tau (hold time) <-> gap to next request; 'spin succeeded' <-> next request arrived while hot; owner_on_cpu <-> probed kernel in flight (launch-hook CUDA events); need_resched <-> watcher got preempted (getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD).ru_nivcsw delta or /proc/thread-self/schedstat run_delay delta), checked at each ~100 us evtstrm wake.

A combined policy suggested by the sources (not tested): WFE only while (kernel in flight) AND (runnable tasks < 6, Go canSpin) AND (no preemption seen since last check, kernel need_resched); on preemption latch NONSPINNABLE (rwsem) until the next launch or until run_delay stays flat for some periods; outside WFE use the timer-slack-1us short sleeps with an M100-style cap; hot window after a request sized by KVM grow/shrink or Lim-Agarwal 0.54 B, with a floor of ~10-20 us so warp-lane bursts (~9 us apart) stay hot. This attacks W's two measured costs (14% load loss, >1 ms tail) the way the kernel does: give up spinning when the CPU is contended.

Board facts checked from running config/source: CONFIG_PREEMPT=y, HZ=250, CONFIG_PSI not set (no /proc/pressure), CONFIG_SCHED_INFO=y and CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS=y, CONFIG_ARM_ARCH_TIMER_EVTSTREAM=y with ARCH_TIMER_EVT_STREAM_PERIOD_US=100, no FEAT_WFxT in /proc/cpuinfo (so no WFET). Derived (not read from debugfs): EEVDF base slice = 0.7 ms x (1 + ilog2(min(ncpu,8))) = 0.7 x 3 = 2.1 ms on 6 CPUs (kernel/sched/fair.c l.76 + get_update_sysctl_factor, SCHED_TUNABLESCALING_LOG), which bounds how long a preempted watcher may wait behind a CPU-bound task.

Unverified / estimates: cost of getrusage, /proc/loadavg, /proc/stat and schedstat reads on this board (estimated us-scale, not measured); YIELD being a no-op on A78AE; DPDK rte_power_monitor using WFE on arm64; Ousterhout 1982 primary text; the Go sysmon timer-slack effect.
