family: User-space poll-mode runtimes that trade latency for CPU or power (DPDK PMD power management and l3fwd-power, SPDK reactors and dynamic scheduler, Seastar reactor, Shenango/Caladan, Arachne, Snap), plus the adaptive-poll kernel mechanisms they borrow from (KVM halt-polling, cpuidle haltpoll, io_uring SQPOLL/hybrid iopoll, NAPI busy-poll/IRQ suspension) and CUDA's own sync-scheduling flags

mechanisms.name: DPDK PMD power mgmt: empty-poll gate (queue_can_sleep / lcore_can_sleep)
mechanisms.where: dpdk main lib/power/rte_power_pmd_mgmt.c (fetched 2026-11-11): queue_can_sleep, lcore_can_sleep, queue_reset, RTE_INIT(rte_power_ethdev_pmgmt_init)
mechanisms.algorithm: An Rx callback runs after every rte_eth_rx_burst. If nb_rx>0, queue_reset() sets n_empty_polls=0 and n_sleeps=0 and leaves the ready-to-sleep set. On an empty poll, n_empty_polls++. If n_empty_polls <= emptypoll_max the core does not sleep, so it keeps busy-polling. Default emptypoll_max=512 (RTE_INIT), changed with rte_power_pmd_mgmt_set_emptypoll_max(). Past the threshold the queue joins the ready set for the current sleep_target epoch. lcore_can_sleep() returns true only when n_queues_ready_to_sleep == n_queues, then resets the count and does sleep_target++. Per-queue empty counters are NOT reset after a sleep, so the core sleeps on every poll until traffic arrives. The threshold is a count of polls, not a time. 512 polls of a NIC ring take roughly tens of microseconds (not measured here).
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Same structure as policy N's hot window (spin, then go to the low-power wait), but counted in polls of flag1 rather than time. One poll of a cached flag costs about 10 ns until the GPU store invalidates the line, so 512 polls is only about 5-10 us of spinning, much shorter than N's 200 us. The 'keep sleeping on every poll until traffic, no re-arm of the spin' rule matches what W already does. Signal needed: none beyond flag1. Cost on this board: the spin itself is one full core for its length. It adds nothing new except evidence that a production runtime uses a very short spin before monitor-wait.

mechanisms.name: DPDK monitor mode: rte_power_monitor (UMONITOR/UMWAIT on x86, LDXR+WFE on Arm), rte_power_monitor_multi (TSX), rte_power_monitor_wakeup
mechanisms.where: dpdk main lib/eal/arm/rte_power_intrinsics.c; lib/eal/arm/include/rte_pause_64.h; lib/eal/x86/rte_power_intrinsics.c; lib/eal/arm/rte_cpuflags.c rte_cpu_get_intrinsics_support; clb_umwait/clb_multiwait/get_monitor_callback/check_monitor in rte_power_pmd_mgmt.c; doc/guides/prog_guide/power_man.rst
mechanisms.algorithm: After emptypoll_max, clb_umwait gets the NIC descriptor address with rte_eth_get_monitor_addr() and calls rte_power_monitor(&pmc, UINT64_MAX), which has no timeout. On Arm64 it does an exclusive load (ldxr/ldxrb/ldxrh by size, relaxed) and then 'wfe', or 'wfet' with the TSC deadline only if RTE_CPUFLAG_WFXT is set. The Arm path never calls pmc->fn to compare the loaded value before sleeping, so wake-ups come from the monitor being cleared, an SEV, an interrupt or the event stream. On Arm, rte_cpu_get_intrinsics_support() sets only power_monitor=1, so rte_power_monitor_multi returns -ENOTSUP and rte_power_pause returns -ENOTSUP. check_monitor() therefore limits monitor mode to one queue per lcore. rte_power_monitor_wakeup on Arm executes 'sev', which wakes all cores. On x86 the sequence is: lock, UMONITOR addr, unlock, read the value, call pmc->fn(value) and abort if the condition is met, otherwise UMWAIT(state C0.2, TSC deadline). AMD uses MONITORX/MWAITX(C1, timeout enable). Wakeup on x86 does a no-op CAS on the monitored address under the per-lcore lock. Multi-address waiting on x86 uses an RTM transaction: XBEGIN, read every address and the lock into the read set, TPAUSE, XEND, so any write aborts the transaction. RTE_ARM_USE_WFE (WFE inside rte_wait_until_equal) is commented out and off by default in config/arm/meson.build.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: On this board DPDK monitor mode is exactly our policy W: /proc/cpuinfo shows 'evtstrm' and no 'wfxt' on all 6 cores, so it is a bare LDXR+WFE with no timeout. The 100 us event stream (ARCH_TIMER_EVT_STREAM_PERIOD_US 100, verified in local kernel headers) bounds each WFE. So DPDK confirms W is the industry-standard design, but it also inherits W's problem: the thread stays runnable and owns the core. DPDK assumes a dedicated, pinned lcore and has no contention detection at all. Unlike DPDK, we should re-check flag1 after LDXR before the WFE, which the x86 path does and the Arm path skips, to close the lost-wakeup window. Check to make: the GPU store and flag1 must fall in the same exclusive-reservation granule (CTR_EL0.ERG, likely 64 B on A78AE, not verified). If bpftime ever has more than one request slot, one WFE covers only one granule, and Arm has no TSX-style multi-address wait. Cost: one full core per watcher while armed, as already measured (-14% for 6 CPU-bound threads).

mechanisms.name: DPDK pause mode (clb_pause): TPAUSE or calibrated rte_pause loop
mechanisms.where: rte_power_pmd_mgmt.c clb_pause, calc_tsc; pause_duration default 1 (RTE_INIT); rte_power_pmd_mgmt_set_pause_duration
mechanisms.algorithm: After the same empty-poll gate, it pauses pause_duration us (default 1 us). If TPAUSE is supported (x86 WAITPKG), it calls rte_power_pause(rdtsc + tsc_per_us*duration) in C0.2. Otherwise it runs a loop of pause_per_us*duration rte_pause() calls, where pause_per_us is calibrated at init by timing 10000 rte_pause() against the TSC. On Arm rte_power_pause is -ENOTSUP, so this is the rte_pause() loop ('yield' hint), which is still busy CPU.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: No benefit on this board. It is a spin with a hint instruction, so the core stays 100% busy and runnable, the same as or worse than W for co-runners. Do not adopt. It does show that DPDK has no time-based OS sleep mode in the PMD library; that only exists in l3fwd-power's epoll path.

mechanisms.name: DPDK scale mode (clb_scale_freq)
mechanisms.where: rte_power_pmd_mgmt.c clb_scale_freq; scale_freq_min default 0 / scale_freq_max UINT32_MAX (unused unless set)
mechanisms.algorithm: Any non-empty poll calls rte_power_freq_max(lcore) immediately. Once the queue and lcore pass the empty-poll gate it calls rte_power_freq_min(lcore). This is asymmetric: scale up on the first packet, scale down only after more than 512 empty polls on all queues. The doc notes it reacts more slowly than pause or monitor mode.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Not applicable. The watcher's cost is scheduler occupancy, not frequency, and per-core DVFS on Orin is per-cluster and pinned by jetson_clocks during our measurements. Signal would be flag1 activity. Skip.

mechanisms.name: l3fwd-power legacy heuristics (main_intr_loop / main_legacy_loop, power_idle_heuristic, power_freq_scaleup_heuristic, power_timer_cb)
mechanisms.where: dpdk main examples/l3fwd-power/main.c lines ~59-67, 115, 430-470, 773-830, 832-870, 920-1080
mechanisms.algorithm: Per queue, zero_rx_packet_count++ on an empty burst. While count <= MIN_ZERO_POLL_COUNT (10) it keeps polling. After that idle_hint = power_idle_heuristic(count): count < SUSPEND_THRESHOLD (300) gives MINIMUM_SLEEP_TIME = 1 us, else 300. The lcore takes the minimum hint over its queues. If hint < 300 it calls rte_delay_us(hint), a busy delay chosen to avoid a context switch that the comment says takes hundreds of us. Otherwise, if interrupts are enabled, it enables Rx interrupts, calls rte_epoll_wait(..., timeout 10 ms), then disables interrupts and goes back to polling. A non-empty burst resets the count. Frequency-down timer: every 1/TIMER_NUMBER_PER_SECOND = 100 ms (SCALING_PERIOD 100000 us). If sleep_time/SCALING_PERIOD >= 0.25 (SCALING_DOWN_TIME_RATIO_THRESHOLD), or average packets per loop iteration < MAX_PKT_BURST (32), it steps frequency down. Up: rxq_count > 96 jumps to the highest frequency; > 64 adds 100 to trend, > 32 adds 1; trend > 10000 steps up one level.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the closest DPDK analog to our old policy N: poll, short busy delays, then block with a timeout. For us the block step does not exist because the GPU cannot raise an IRQ for flag1, so their 10 ms epoll becomes our periodic sleep. Useful pieces: (a) a 2-stage threshold on consecutive empty checks (10 then 300) instead of a time window; (b) the 100 ms supervisory timer that downgrades when sleep ratio >= 25%, the same shape as an epoch controller for picking S-period vs M100. Signals: count of empty flag1 checks and the watcher's own sleep ratio. Cost: negligible bookkeeping.

mechanisms.name: DPDK legacy empty-poll API (training-based, removed)
mechanisms.where: dpdk v22.07 lib/power/rte_power_empty_poll.c (present in v22.11, 404 from v23.03 on)
mechanisms.algorithm: INTERVALS_PER_SECOND 100 (10 ms intervals), SECONDS_TO_TRAIN_FOR 2. A training phase measures base_edpi, the empty dequeues per interval when idle. At run time, percent busy = 100 - avg(edpi over BINS_AV=4 intervals)/base_edpi*100. In MED, percent > 70 (DEFAULT_MED_TO_HIGH_PERCENT_THRESHOLD) for more than 100 consecutive intervals (1 s) moves to HGH. In HGH, percent < 30 for 1 s moves back to MED.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Shows the 'busy % from empty-poll rate' estimator and its 1 s hysteresis. Removed upstream because of training fragility. For us: request rate per epoch is a cleaner input than empty-poll counts. Not recommended beyond the hysteresis idea.

mechanisms.name: SPDK reactor poll/interrupt mode + dynamic scheduler
mechanisms.where: spdk master lib/event/reactor.c (_reactor_run, reactor_run, reactor_interrupt_run, get_rusage, CONTEXT_SWITCH_MONITOR_PERIOD); module/scheduler/dynamic/scheduler_dynamic.c (g_scheduler_load_limit=20, core_limit=80, core_busy=95, balance); lib/event/app_rpc.c (default period); doc/scheduler.md
mechanisms.algorithm: Each reactor loop polls its spdk_threads. Pollers return BUSY or IDLE, and the tsc since the last iteration is charged to busy_tsc (rc>0) or idle_tsc (rc==0). The scheduler runs every scheduler period on the scheduling reactor. framework_set_scheduler sets 1 s (SPDK_SEC_TO_USEC) if no period is given. The static scheduler is the default and does no rebalancing. Dynamic scheduler: thread load = busy/(busy+idle)*100. Threads with load < load_limit (20%) move to the main core. Active threads are spread so no core exceeds core_limit (80%). A core at or above core_busy (95%) counts as overloaded. Reactors left with zero threads switch to interrupt mode: reactor_interrupt_run calls spdk_fd_group_wait(fgrp, -1), an epoll that blocks forever until an eventfd or timerfd fires. The main core gets governor freq up/down by busy>idle. Context-switch monitor: every 1 s (CONTEXT_SWITCH_MONITOR_PERIOD 1000000 us) getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD) logs ru_nvcsw/ru_nivcsw deltas at INFO level only. No action is taken on contention.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Two ideas transfer. (1) The busy/idle tsc accounting per epoch, with a 20% load floor before a 'core' (for us, a hot-polling mode) is granted: watcher busy fraction = time spent serving requests / epoch, and if < 20% the watcher should not hold a hot core. (2) The getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD).ru_nivcsw delta as a coarse contention flag. SPDK only logs it. Cost here: one getrusage syscall, about 1 us (estimate, not measured), fine at 1-10 ms epochs. The interrupt-mode half (epoll -1 on an eventfd) has no equivalent for flag1. Nothing on the CPU can be woken by a GPU store except the WFE exclusive monitor. The only 'interrupt' we can get is a CUDA event at a kernel boundary (blocking-sync), so SPDK's park point maps to 'no probed kernel in flight'. Like DPDK, SPDK assumes pinned dedicated reactors.

mechanisms.name: Seastar reactor: idle poll then sleep (idle-poll-time-us, overprovisioned, poll-mode)
mechanisms.where: scylladb/seastar master src/core/reactor.cc: reactor::do_run loop (~3440-3510), calculate_poll_time (~5028), reactor_options (~4057-4077), reactor_config build (~4636-4680), wakeup_granularity (~3960), smp_pollfn::try_enter_interrupt_mode (~3048), reactor::wakeup (~3113)
mechanisms.algorithm: Loop: run tasks, then check_for_work = poll_once() || have_more_tasks(). If there is work, reset idle_poll_start. If not, record idle_poll_start on the first empty poll and cpu_relax(). Once now - idle_poll_start > max_poll_time, call pollers_enter_interrupt_mode(). Each poller arms its fd source and re-polls (signal poller blocks all signals then re-polls; smp poller sets _sleeping=true, runs try_systemwide_memory_barrier (membarrier), then re-polls; any hit means 'raced', so it undoes and keeps polling). Only then does it disarm the 0.5 ms task-quota timerfd and block in _backend->wait_and_process_events (epoll/io_uring/aio). Senders call reactor::wakeup(), which writes the eventfd only if _sleeping. Tasks that ran after a wakeup do not restart the idle window ('the reactor sleeps again after one empty poll'). max_poll_time: --poll-mode means infinite; --overprovisioned with idle-poll-time-us left at default means 0 us; otherwise idle_poll_time_us, whose default is calculate_poll_time() = 200 us on bare metal and 2000 us when virtualized ('competitive with halt/unhalt'). --overprovisioned is documented as '--idle-poll-time-us 0 --thread-affinity 0 --poll-aio 0'. Safety check: if sched_wakeup_granularity (from /proc/sys/kernel/sched_wakeup_granularity_ns or debugfs) is >= 15 ms, it forces max_poll_time=0 and poll-aio off (seastar issue #2696, so polling does not starve helper threads).
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Our N's 200 us hot window is the same number as Seastar's bare-metal default, and Seastar picks 200 us to match halt/unhalt cost, not request gaps. Seastar's own answer to sharing cores is the operator flag --overprovisioned, which sets the poll window to 0. That is our M100/S-n without a hot window, consistent with our finding that M100 is best under full load. Its automatic contention check does not work here: Linux 6.8 is EEVDF, /proc/sys/kernel/sched_wakeup_granularity_ns does not exist on this board (verified), and debugfs needs root, so it would read 0 and never trigger. Transferable rule: 'after a burst, go back to sleep after ONE empty check, not a full hot window'. The 'announce sleeping, barrier, re-check' handshake would only matter if the GPU could read a 'watcher sleeping' flag, and it cannot wake us anyway. Cost: none to adopt the window rule.

mechanisms.name: Shenango IOKernel congestion detection (5 us, two consecutive checks) + runtime park after 2 us
mechanisms.where: Ousterhout et al., NSDI'19 (usenix.org/system/files/nsdi19-ousterhout.pdf) section 4.1, Algorithm 1, section 6.1, section 7.3 'Core allocation interval'; shenango/shenango master iokernel/main.c CORES_ADJUST_INTERVAL_US 5; iokernel/cores.c cores_is_proc_congested; runtime/defs.h RUNTIME_SCHED_POLL_ITERS 4, RUNTIME_SCHED_MIN_POLL_US 2; runtime/sched.c schedule()
mechanisms.algorithm: A dedicated IOKernel core runs cores_adjust_assignments every 5 us. For each active kthread it compares the current runqueue/ingress tail with the head saved at the previous check: wraps_lt(rq_tail, last_rq_head), meaning an item that was queued 5 us ago is still unprocessed. That marks the process congested and grants one core (guaranteed first, then burstable). A thread that just woke gets a one-round pass (th->waking). The paper argues queueing duration is more robust than queue length because length needs a per-workload threshold. Runtime side: with no local work it tries work stealing (sibling, random, all). It parks only after RUNTIME_SCHED_POLL_ITERS (4) iterations AND RUNTIME_SCHED_MIN_POLL_US (2 us) of finding nothing. Parking means a command-queue message to the IOKernel plus a blocking read on an eventfd. Unpark is an eventfd write; preempt is SIGUSR1 via tgkill. Measured: a 5 us interval vs 25/50/100 us costs the batch app up to 6% throughput but avoids at least +150 us tail latency; intervals below 5 us improved latency only marginally while wasting cycles parking; Linux process switch about 600 ns.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The 'same item seen at two consecutive checks' rule maps directly: if flag1 is already set when the watcher wakes, a request waited up to one period, and if the watcher sees a backlog (a second request already posted, or flag1 still set after serving one, e.g. the next warp lane) it should shorten its period or switch to hot polling for the burst. This is a zero-cost, request-driven escalation signal with no thresholds to tune. The 2 us min spin before parking is Shenango's spin-then-block window. Our analog is the hot window after a request, which should cover the ~9 us lane spacing (so about 10-20 us), not 200 us. Shenango's dedicated 5 us poller core is exactly what we cannot afford (it is W). The eventfd park/unpark has no flag1 equivalent.

mechanisms.name: Caladan top-level core allocator: queueing delay of oldest element vs THRESH_QD, 10 us loop
mechanisms.where: Fried et al., OSDI'20 (pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/caladan:osdi20.pdf) section 5.2.1 Algorithm 1, section 5.3 KSCHED, Appendix A; shenango/caladan main iokernel/defs.h IOKERNEL_POLL_INTERVAL 10; iokernel/sched.c sched_measure_kthread_delay, calc_delay_tsc; iokernel/simple.c simple_notify_congested; runtime/defs.h RUNTIME_SCHED_POLL_ITERS 0, RUNTIME_SCHED_MIN_POLL_US 2; runtime/cfg.c runtime_qdelay_us
mechanisms.algorithm: Every IOKERNEL_POLL_INTERVAL = 10 us the scheduler core reads per-kthread shared-memory queue state. Delay per kthread = sum over its queues (uthread runqueue, RX queue, timers, directpath, storage) of now - timestamp of the oldest element. Each element carries its arrival TSC (oldest_tsc), and the RX side uses rxq_busy_since as an approximation. Task delay = max over its kthreads. In simple.c, congested = (qdelay_us==0 ? standing_queue : max_delay_us >= qdelay_us) || parked_thread_busy. standing_queue = the Shenango two-consecutive-checks rule, or a timer overdue by more than 10 us. Skipped if a core was woken in the last interval. A congested process tries simple_add_kthread at once, else joins the congested list for later cores. Paper default THRESH_QD = 10 us. A THRESH_QD of 100 us gives +7% best-effort throughput for +54 us LC tail, and values below 10 us hurt BE throughput with no tail gain. Runtime parks after RUNTIME_SCHED_MIN_POLL_US 2 us (iters threshold 0). KSCHED idles a parked core with MONITOR/MWAIT (C1) on a 64-byte per-core command line packed contiguously, so the scheduler's write wakes it. The paper notes mwait 'requires a few microseconds to park a hyperthread'.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The best signal from this family for us is per-request queueing delay. Have the probe write the GPU %globaltimer (ns) into the request slot when it sets flag1. The watcher computes service delay = now - posted per call and keeps an EWMA or max per epoch. Caveat: aligning GPU globaltimer with CPU CLOCK_MONOTONIC on Orin is not verified and needs a one-time offset calibration. The rule becomes Caladan's: if the max delay in an epoch exceeds THRESH (e.g. 100 us, our latency budget), escalate (shorter period, or WFE while a kernel is in flight); if it stays far below, relax. This also lets us fit the sqrt model online: lambda from the request count per epoch, mean wait from the measured delays. Cost: one 8-byte store per request on the GPU (negligible next to the ~10 us service) and one clock_gettime (vDSO, about 50 ns) on the CPU. Instrumentation only (read-only task). KSCHED's mwait-on-command-line is the x86 twin of W, and it relies on a dedicated core.

mechanisms.name: Arachne core estimator (load factor up, utilization down, hysteresis)
mechanisms.where: Qin et al., OSDI'18 (usenix.org/system/files/osdi18-qin.pdf) section 6.2; PlatformLab/Arachne master src/CoreLoadEstimator.cc/.h (loadFactorThreshold 1.5, maxUtilization 0.8, idleCoreFractionHysteresis 0.09, zeroCoreUtilizationThreshold 0.01), src/DefaultCorePolicy.h measurementPeriod 50*1000*1000 (ns, 50 ms), src/Arachne.cc idleCycles/weightedLoadedCycles accounting
mechanisms.algorithm: Every 50 ms: utilization = (totalCycles - idleCycles)/measurementCycles, in cores; load factor = weightedLoadedCycles/totalCycles, the average number of runnable user threads. Scale up by one core if averageLoadFactor > 1.5, and record utilizationThresholds[curCores] = current total utilization. Scale down by one if utilization < max(0.01, utilizationThresholds[curCores-1] - 0.09*(curCores-1)), i.e. back below the level that triggered the last increase, minus 9% hysteresis per core. Alternative UTILIZATION strategy: up if util > 0.8*cores, down if util < 0.8*(cores-1) - 0.09. The arbiter forcibly reclaims a core if it is not released within 10 ms. The paper says load factor works better than utilization for scaling up, because one threshold fits many workloads.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Two transferable ideas. (1) The asymmetric controller: escalate on a latency-type signal (load factor, or for us the measured request delay), de-escalate on a utilization signal (watcher busy fraction) with the threshold remembered from the escalation point plus hysteresis. This avoids flapping between S-period/W and M100. (2) The 'load factor' of the CPU itself is available to us. Per-CPU field 8 of /proc/schedstat (sum of runqueue wait ns on that CPU) as a delta over an epoch, divided by the epoch, is about the average number of waiting tasks, which is Arachne's load factor minus the running one. Verified populated on this board even with kernel.sched_schedstats=0 (CONFIG_SCHED_INFO=y). Cost: reading /proc/schedstat is a procfs open+read, several us (estimate), so use it only at 10-50 ms epochs, never per wake-up. Arachne's dispatcher spins when idle (not verified in detail), so its per-core idle path is not a model for us.

mechanisms.name: Snap engine scheduling modes: dedicated (spin, optional mwait), spreading (block on interrupt, MicroQuanta RT class), compacting (poll queueing delay, rebalance, block after idleness)
mechanisms.where: Marty et al., SOSP'19 'Snap: a Microkernel Approach to Host Networking' (courses.grainger.illinois.edu/ece598hpn/fa2023/papers/snap.pdf) sections 2.4, 2.4.1, 5.2, 5.3, 6.3
mechanisms.algorithm: Dedicated cores: engines pinned and spin-polling, 'optionally invoking a userspace mwait to conserve power'. Spreading: each engine has its own thread that 'schedules only when active and blocks on interrupt notification when idle'. Wake-up comes from the NIC or an application syscall, and threads run in MicroQuanta, a kernel class giving 'runtime out of every period' with per-CPU hrtimers for microsecond-granularity slicing, so they preempt CFS. Compacting: engines run on as few threads as possible while 'queueing delay ... measured using an algorithm similar to Shenango' stays below an SLO. A periodic rebalance scales out on queue build-up and migrates back on low load. It 'supports blocking on interrupt notification after some period of idleness'. Measured: spreading has worse latency at low QPS because of C-state interrupt wake-up, and compacting avoids that because its least-loaded state spin-polls one core. Under an mmap/munmap antagonist, compacting is best. MicroQuanta beats CFS nice -20 under antagonists (Fig 6d). NOT VERIFIED / not published: the compacting rebalance period, the idle period before blocking, and the queueing-delay SLO value.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Snap's answer to tail latency under CPU contention is the scheduling class, not the polling policy. For our sleep-based policies (M100, S50), the 1-3.5% (and W's 13-31%) of calls waiting >1 ms are about one 4 ms tick of runqueue wait (HZ=250). Putting the watcher in SCHED_FIFO (or SCHED_DEADLINE with a small runtime/period) would make each timer wake-up preempt CFS load immediately. That is a candidate experiment for later, not run. It does not help W: an RT thread spinning in WFE still owns the core and would starve CFS until RT throttling (sched_rt_runtime_us 950000/1000000). At M100's 0.02-0.1 core, RT throttling is irrelevant. Needs CAP_SYS_NICE or RLIMIT_RTPRIO. The compacting idea of polling queueing delay and only then holding a core matches the Caladan signal above.

mechanisms.name: KVM adaptive halt-polling (per-vCPU grow/shrink) with single_task_running gate
mechanisms.where: Linux v6.8 virt/kvm/kvm_main.c kvm_vcpu_halt, grow_halt_poll_ns, shrink_halt_poll_ns, module params; include/linux/kvm_host.h kvm_vcpu_can_poll; arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_host.h KVM_HALT_POLL_NS_DEFAULT 500000 (x86: 200000); Documentation/virt/kvm/halt-polling.rst
mechanisms.algorithm: On a guest halt, poll for vcpu->halt_poll_ns while kvm_vcpu_can_poll(): single_task_running() && !need_resched() && now < stop. Polling stops as soon as anything else wants the CPU. If nothing arrives, it blocks. Afterwards, with halt_ns the total halt time: invalid wake-up means shrink; halt_ns <= poll_ns means poll succeeded and nothing changes; poll_ns>0 and halt_ns > max (500 us on arm64) means a long block, so shrink; poll_ns < max and halt_ns < max means a short halt with too small a window, so grow. grow: val *= halt_poll_ns_grow (2), raised to at least halt_poll_ns_grow_start (10000 ns). shrink: halt_poll_ns_shrink default 0 resets to 0, else divide, and anything below grow_start becomes 0. Polling counts as successful if the vCPU never actually scheduled out.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The direct replacement for N's fixed 200 us hot window: an adaptive window per watcher. After a request: if the next request came within the window, keep it; if it came just after the window ended but before a long gap (< cap), double it (from 10 us); if the gap exceeded the cap, reset to 0. With warp lanes about 9 us apart, this should converge to about 10-20 us during bursts and 0 between launches. That is the Karlin-style window, a hypothesis to check by replaying recorded request timestamps offline. The single_task_running()/need_resched() gate is the in-kernel contention check that user space cannot read directly. Our user-space equivalent is the sleep-overshoot signal (see notes). Cost: a few compares per request.

mechanisms.name: cpuidle haltpoll governor (guest-side adaptive poll)
mechanisms.where: Linux v6.8 drivers/cpuidle/governors/haltpoll.c adjust_poll_limit and module params; drivers/cpuidle/poll_state.c POLL_IDLE_RELAX_COUNT 200
mechanisms.algorithm: guest_halt_poll_ns = 200000 (cap). If block_ns > poll_limit_ns and block_ns <= cap, poll_limit = poll_limit*guest_halt_poll_grow (2), at least guest_halt_poll_grow_start (50000 ns), at most the cap. If block_ns > cap and allow_shrink, poll_limit /= guest_halt_poll_shrink (2), where 0 means reset. The poll loop checks need_resched and the time limit every 200 cpu_relax iterations.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Same adaptive scheme as KVM but with a gentler shrink (/2 instead of reset) and a larger grow_start (50 us). Our request pattern (bursts, then gaps of a launch or more) favors KVM's reset-to-0 shrink, so we do not pay a hot window after the last lane of a burst. Cost: trivial.

mechanisms.name: io_uring SQPOLL idle timeout and hybrid iopoll
mechanisms.where: Linux v6.8 io_uring/sqpoll.c (sq_thread_idle, need_resched, IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP, default HZ); hybrid: Linux master io_uring/rw.c io_hybrid_iopoll_delay / io_uring_hybrid_poll (present in v6.13, absent in v6.12; not in this board's 6.8)
mechanisms.algorithm: SQPOLL: the kernel thread polls the SQ, resetting timeout = jiffies + sq_thread_idle on work (default: sq_thread_idle = msecs_to_jiffies(param), 0 meaning HZ = 1 s). It yields on need_resched(). After idle it sets IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP in sq_flags and sleeps, and user space must then call io_uring_enter(SQ_WAKEUP). Hybrid iopoll: the first poll is pure spinning, then sleep hybrid_poll_time/2 with an hrtimer and spin for the rest. hybrid_poll_time = the minimum observed (runtime - sleep), shrinking only.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: SQPOLL's NEED_WAKEUP is the 'tell the producer the consumer is asleep' protocol. The GPU could read such a flag, but it has no way to wake the CPU, so this does not apply mid-kernel. Hybrid iopoll maps to the timing within a burst: after serving lane k, sleep about half the observed inter-lane gap (~4 us at our 9 us spacing) then poll, which saves part of the 9 us per lane. On this board a sleep has a fixed overhead of about +4 us and about 1.2 us of CPU, so for 9 us gaps the gain is small. Note only.

mechanisms.name: NAPI busy-poll / deferred hard IRQs / IRQ suspension
mechanisms.where: Linux master Documentation/networking/napi.rst (busy_poll, busy_read, SO_BUSY_POLL, gro_flush_timeout, napi_defer_hard_irqs, prefer_busy_poll, irq-suspend-timeout)
mechanisms.algorithm: napi_defer_hard_irqs = the number of consecutive empty polls before hardware IRQs are re-enabled, with gro_flush_timeout as the repoll timer in the meantime. prefer_busy_poll: the app promises to busy-poll and IRQs stay masked, and the promise is revoked 'if gro_flush_timeout passes without any busy poll call'. irq-suspend-timeout (per NAPI, ns): while epoll_wait keeps returning events, IRQs stay suspended and each successful return re-arms the timer. When epoll_wait finds nothing, suspension ends and the defer/timeout path takes over. The timeout is a safety net and should be 'much larger than' gro_flush_timeout. No defaults are given in the doc.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The idea of 'stay in poll mode only while each poll finds work, fall back after N empty polls, with a watchdog timeout' is the same structure as our hot window keyed to request arrivals. Not directly usable because there is no IRQ for flag1. Conceptual support for a work-driven (not time-driven) hot window.

mechanisms.name: CUDA context scheduling flags (spin / yield / blocking-sync / auto)
mechanisms.where: /usr/local/cuda-13.2/include/cuda.h CUctx_flags_enum and cuCtxCreate docs (lines ~381-389, ~6147-6157); cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState
mechanisms.algorithm: CU_CTX_SCHED_AUTO (0) uses a heuristic on active contexts C vs logical processors P: if C > P use YIELD, else SPIN. Also documented: 'on Tegra devices, CU_CTX_SCHED_AUTO uses a heuristic based on the power profile of the platform and may choose CU_CTX_SCHED_BLOCKING_SYNC for low-powered devices'. SPIN=1, YIELD=2, BLOCKING_SYNC=4, mask 7.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Matches our observation that Auto behaves as blocking sync on this Orin. NVIDIA itself chose blocking over spinning for host waits on Tegra power profiles, which supports not holding a core with W by default. The app's flags, read with cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState (cheap, once per context), can be a policy input. If the app chose SPIN, it already burns a core waiting on the GPU, so W costs the system less relative to that. If BLOCKING_SYNC or AUTO-on-Tegra, prefer sleep-based (M100/S-n). Blocking-sync CUDA events are also the only true 'interrupt mode' park point available to the watcher: it can block until a probed kernel ends, but not until flag1 is set.

notes:
Cross-cutting conclusions (all sources read 2026-11-11; local copies under /tmp/claude-2002/-home-jetson-src/6ac0883f-4479-466c-bec5-5fa31cffe4de/scratchpad/poll-survey/{dpdk,spdk,seastar,shenango,caladan,arachne,linux,papers}).

1) The discriminating axis is whether a design shares the core. DPDK PMD mgmt, SPDK reactors, Shenango/Caladan IOKernel and KSCHED, and Snap dedicated mode all assume a dedicated, pinned core, and none detects CPU contention. SPDK's getrusage nivcsw monitor only logs it. Only KVM halt-poll (in-kernel single_task_running && !need_resched), Seastar (--overprovisioned sets the poll window to 0, plus a sched_wakeup_granularity >= 15 ms check) and Snap (MicroQuanta RT class) address shared cores. On this board Seastar's automatic check is dead: 6.8 is EEVDF and /proc/sys/kernel/sched_wakeup_granularity_ns does not exist (verified).

2) There is no 'interrupt mode' for flag1. Every park/unpark in the family (Shenango eventfd read, SPDK epoll -1, Seastar epoll + eventfd, Snap interrupt notification, io_uring NEED_WAKEUP) needs the producer to raise a CPU-side wake-up. The GPU cannot do that mid-kernel. The only CPU-side wake-up from a GPU store is the WFE exclusive monitor (policy W). So the design space is {WFE while we are allowed to hold a core, periodic sleep}. The only true block is at kernel boundaries (blocking-sync CUDA event), which our data says costs more than it saves at ~100% GPU busy. DPDK's Arm monitor mode is literally W (LDXR + bare WFE; no WFxT on this A78AE: /proc/cpuinfo shows evtstrm but not wfxt; event stream 100 us per local arm_arch_timer.h), and DPDK's Arm 'pause' mode is a busy rte_pause loop.

3) Contention signals usable on this board, cheapest first:
 (a) Sleep overshoot, free. A nanosleep(n) with 1 us slack returns at about n+4 us when uncontended (our measurement). overshoot = (t_wake - t_sleep) - n - 4 us, read with vDSO clock_gettime (about 50 ns), is the watcher's own runqueue delay on every wake-up. It is the user-space analog of KVM's need_resched gate. Proposed primary signal, e.g. EWMA of overshoot > ~50 us means contended.
 (b) /proc/thread-self/schedstat field 2 (run_delay ns) and getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD).ru_nivcsw (the SPDK pattern). Verified populated on this board with kernel.sched_schedstats=0 because CONFIG_SCHED_INFO=y and CONFIG_SCHEDSTATS=y. Cost: procfs open/read is several us and getrusage about 1 us (estimates, not measured). Use at 1-50 ms epochs as confirmation, not per wake-up.
 (c) Per-CPU /proc/schedstat field 8 (runqueue wait ns per CPU), delta over epoch: system-wide, Arachne-style load factor. Several us, epoch-only.
 (d) PSI (/proc/pressure/cpu) is NOT available: CONFIG_PSI is not set (verified). /proc/stat procs_running is global and coarse.
 Request-side signals: request rate per epoch (lambda for T* = sqrt(2c/(alpha*lambda))); Shenango's two-consecutive-checks rule (flag1 already set on wake-up, or the next lane already posted means escalate); Caladan's per-request queueing delay, which needs the GPU to stamp %globaltimer into the request (GPU-CPU clock alignment on Orin not verified); CUDA launch events; CUDA ctx sched flags via cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState.

4) Concrete policy shape suggested by the family (not tested):
 - Hot window after each request: KVM-style adaptive (grow x2 from 10 us when the next request arrived just after the window, reset to 0 when the gap exceeds the cap). Expected to settle at about 10-20 us for 9 us lane spacing instead of N's fixed 200 us, which equals Seastar's bare-metal default chosen for halt/unhalt cost, not request gaps.
 - Between bursts: periodic sleep with period chosen per epoch by the sqrt model from the measured lambda and the overshoot/runqueue-delay signal (Arachne-style asymmetric controller: escalate on measured request delay > budget, de-escalate on busy fraction below the remembered escalation level minus hysteresis, e.g. 9%). Caladan data point: a delay threshold of 10 us vs 100 us traded 7% batch throughput for 54 us of tail.
 - W only when the overshoot signal says the CPU has an idle core, and CUDA ctx flags/launch tracking say a probed kernel is in flight.
 - Tail fix candidate (Snap lesson): SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_DEADLINE for a sleep-based watcher removes the ~4 ms (HZ=250) CFS wait behind CPU-bound threads. Not applicable to W.

5) Not verified / not found: published power or latency numbers for DPDK monitor/pause/scale modes (none found); Snap compacting-mode constants (rebalance period, idle time before blocking, delay SLO), which are not in the paper; Arachne dispatcher idle behaviour beyond the estimator constants; Shenango paper's per-operation park/unpark cost in us (only Fig. 6 qualitative 'a few us'); A78AE exclusive-reservation granule size (CTR_EL0.ERG, likely 64 B); costs of procfs reads and getrusage on this board (estimates only; no benchmarks run per task constraints). The io_uring hybrid iopoll is v6.13+ (absent in 6.8). The DPDK empty-poll API exists in v22.11 and was removed in v23.03.

family: GPU-to-CPU callbacks and host-side polling in GPU systems (proxy/progress threads, GPU RPC servers, GPU system calls, GPU-to-CPU interrupts, CUDA sync internals on Jetson)

mechanisms.name: NCCL proxy progress thread: blocks on a condition variable when no ops are active, busy-polls while they are
mechanisms.where: NVIDIA/nccl master ad2d192c1f27 (2026-11-09), src/proxy.cc: ncclProxyProgress() lines ~956-1015, ncclProxyGetPostedOps() ~834-910, ncclProxyPost() ~481-490
mechanisms.algorithm: Loop: progressOps(active list, &idle). If idle, or nothing is active, or ++counter == NCCL_PROGRESS_APPENDOP_FREQ (default 8), call ncclProxyGetPostedOps(); if it added nothing, call std::this_thread::yield() (sched_yield). In ncclProxyGetPostedOps: if state->active != NULL and (nothing posted or try_lock fails), return at once without blocking. If state->active == NULL, lock the pool mutex and pool->cond.wait(lock, pred: nextOps != -1 || stop). Work is fetched in batches of up to NCCL_PROXY_APPEND_BATCH_SIZE = 16 (opCount,peer) groups. The thread is woken by ncclProxyPost(), which the host-side enqueue path calls when a collective is launched: under the mutex, cond.notify_one() fires only when the pool goes from empty to non-empty (pool->nextOps == -1). There is no timed sleep and no backoff anywhere. The thread spins with yield until every posted op has finished its known number of steps. Affinity can be set with NCCL_PROXY_CPUSET.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is launch tracking done exactly: the CPU-side launch posts work and wakes the proxy, and the proxy blocks (0 CPU) only when nothing is outstanding. NCCL can do this because each op carries a known step count, so it knows when it is finished. bpftime cannot know how many host calls a kernel will make. Its equivalent of 'op finished' is 'probed kernel completed', taken from the CUDA events our launch hooks already record. Signal: count of in-flight probed launches, incremented in the launch hook and decremented on kernel completion. Cost on this board: the same as W/S while a kernel runs (yield-spinning is W-like: about 1 core and the 14% loss under full load), and 0 when idle. NCCL accepts the hot core because collectives are short. For long GPU-bound kernels it reproduces our W problem. Worth taking: the empty-to-non-empty notify_one, which means no wake-up per launch.
mechanisms.measured: No published latency/CPU numbers in source; design intent stated in comments ('Too frequent call of ncclProxyGetPostedOps() will result in perf regression for small message communication').

mechanisms.name: NVSHMEM host proxy thread: pure busy-poll, no sleep, no yield
mechanisms.where: NVIDIA/nvshmem main 2c7f5a37b16d, src/host/proxy/proxy.cpp: nvshmemi_proxy_progress() line 1460, nvshmemi_proxy_progress_minimal() line 1488, progress() ~1440, proxy_update_processed() ~146
mechanisms.algorithm: do { progress(state) } while (!stop), where progress() runs global-exit, quiet, cst, timeout polling (if NVSHMEM_TIMEOUT_DEVICE_POLLING), channels, then transports. Requests sit in a host-pinned ring and every 8-byte entry carries a flag byte that the proxy spins on (while (*(volatile uint8_t*)&req->flag != flag)). The 'processed' credit goes back to the GPU only when processed - last_sync >= 1024 bytes (or on force_update), which batches the reverse-direction writes. Even the 'minimal' proxy level (only global-exit and timeout) spins without sleeping. Proxy level NONE (no thread) is used when every transport is GPU-initiated (P2P or IBGDA).
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the 'dedicate a core' end of the design space (our W without WFE). The only idea to borrow is credit batching: return the completion/credit to the GPU every N bytes, not per request. That only helps one-way requests (printk/ringbuf output), not map lookups that need a reply. Cost on this board: 1 of 6 cores at 100% for the lifetime of the context, worse than W (WFE at least idles the pipeline). Not suitable.
mechanisms.measured: None in source.

mechanisms.name: NVBit channel: GPU-side 1 MB batching plus a host receive thread that spins on a doorbell
mechanisms.where: NVBit v1.8.1 release tarball (github.com/NVlabs/NVBit releases, nvbit-Linux-aarch64-1.8.1.tar.bz2): core/utils/channel.hpp ChannelDev::push/flush_bytes, ChannelHost::recv; tools/mem_trace/mem_trace.cu recv_thread_fun (lines 465-505), CHANNEL_SIZE = 1<<20
mechanisms.algorithm: Device: push() takes space in a 1 MiB buffer with atomic fetch_add on head_bytes and copies the packet. When the buffer is full, one thread waits until tail == head, stores nbytes into a host-mapped int doorbell (system-scope release), then spins until the host writes 0 back. Host: recv() does an acquire-load of the doorbell. If it is 0 it returns 0 immediately. Otherwise it copies the bytes and stores 0. The receive thread calls recv() in a tight while (state == WORKING) loop with no sleep or yield. After each kernel the tool launches a flush_channel kernel and calls cudaDeviceSynchronize, so a partial buffer is drained at kernel end.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: NVBit avoids the latency problem entirely: traces are one-way, so the GPU never waits for the CPU except when the 1 MiB buffer is full. bpftime host calls that need no reply (bpf_printk, perf/ringbuf output) could take this route: batch them in GPU memory, flush at buffer-full or kernel end, and keep the synchronous flag1/flag2 path only for map ops that return values. That shrinks the request rate lambda the watcher must serve, and by the square-root model a smaller lambda means a longer optimal period. The receive thread itself (a spin loop) is W without WFE and should not be copied. Signal: request type in the request header.
mechanisms.measured: None in source.

mechanisms.name: LLVM offload RPC server thread (CUDA and AMDGPU): launch tracking via notify() at launch and cuLaunchHostFunc -> finish(), then sleep 250 us after an empty scan
mechanisms.where: llvm/llvm-project main 74390a6a3f10: offload/plugins-nextgen/common/include/RPC.h ServerThread (SleepFunction default sleep_for(250us), notify(), finish()); common/src/RPC.cpp ServerThread::run() ~146-175; cuda/src/rtl.cpp launchImpl ~1520-1556; history: eea62159e8 'Make the RPC thread sleep briefly when idle' (#168596, 2025-11-19), 4961700c10 'Support AMDGPU device interrupts for the RPC interface' (#188067, 2026-03-24)
mechanisms.algorithm: NumUsers counts kernels in flight that may use RPC. In the CUDA plugin launch path: Thread->notify() (NumUsers++ under a mutex, CV.notify_all) before cuLaunchKernelEx, then cuLaunchHostFunc(stream, [](){ Thread->finish(); }) (NumUsers--) right after it. Server: CV.wait until NumUsers > 0 or shutdown. Then loop while NumUsers > 0: if (!ClientInUse) SleepFunction(); ClientInUse = false; scan every port of every device (ClientInUse = true if any port had work). On NVIDIA, SleepFunction stays the default std::this_thread::sleep_for(250 us). On AMDGPU it becomes a blocking HSA signal wait (next entry). Older version (Nov 2025): IdleTime = 25 us after the last use, then sleep_for(250 us) per scan, reset when work is found. Today's version sleeps 250 us after any empty scan, with no hot window. GPU side (libc/shared/rpc_util.h sleep_briefly): while waiting for its reply the client runs nanosleep.u32 64 on sm_70+, s_sleep 2 on AMDGPU, and isb on ARM.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the closest relative of our policy: S250 plus launch tracking. Two differences matter. (1) Completion tracking uses cuLaunchHostFunc, not polling events every 100 us. A host function is ordered after the kernel and runs on the CUDA driver's callback thread, so the watcher needs no periodic event check and the cost is about one wake per launch. Caveat: cuLaunchHostFunc blocks later work in that stream until it runs ('will block work added after it'), which adds a CPU round trip between back-to-back kernels in the app's stream. Alternatives that avoid stalling the stream: a helper thread calling cuEventSynchronize on an event created with CU_EVENT_BLOCKING_SYNC (it sleeps in the kernel on a host1x interrupt, see the Jetson entries), or the host function enqueued on a separate stream after cuStreamWaitEvent. (2) Their period is fixed at 250 us, picked by hand, which suggests sub-ms latency is acceptable for libc RPC. Our S50/M100 data says the period should depend on load. Signals: in-flight probed launch count (launch hook ++, hostfunc or blocking-event --) plus 'previous scan empty'. Cost on this board: idle 0, busy-kernel-with-no-calls ~1 wake per 254 us (~4 kHz x 1.2 us ≈ 0.5% of a core), latency ~127 us mean random-phase. Hostfunc/event wake latency on Jetson: NOT measured.
mechanisms.measured: PR text only: 'after 25 microseconds we will assume the server is inactive and begin sleeping'; no latency numbers published.

mechanisms.name: LLVM libc RPC doorbell: the GPU interrupts only on the 0->1 transition of an in-flight counter (AMDGPU)
mechanisms.where: llvm/llvm-project main: libc/shared/rpc.h Process::notify()/finish(), struct Doorbell; offload/plugins-nextgen/amdgpu/src/rtl.cpp initRPCDoorbell() ~4487-4525
mechanisms.algorithm: Doorbell = {uint64_t *value, uint64_t *mailbox, uint32_t event_id}, taken from an HSA interrupt signal (value field, event_mailbox_ptr, event_id). Client notify(): the first active lane does old = atomic_fetch_add(value, 1, relaxed, system scope). Only if old == 0 and mailbox != NULL does it store event_id into the mailbox, fence (release), and raise the interrupt (signal_interrupt = s_sendmsg). finish() does fetch_sub(value, 1). Server sleep: hsa_signal_wait_scacquire(signal, NE, 0, UINT64_MAX, HSA_WAIT_STATE_BLOCKED), so it blocks while the in-flight count is 0. Wake on shutdown: hsa_signal_store_screlease(signal, 1). Requests that arrive while another is outstanding raise no interrupt, because the server is already awake and scanning.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the structure we would want if NVIDIA had a GPU-to-CPU interrupt: one interrupt per idle-to-busy transition, then polling until the count returns to 0. That fits our bursts (32 lanes about 9 us apart give 1 interrupt, not 32). On NVIDIA/Jetson no documented in-kernel interrupt exists (see the nvgpu/host1x entries). The counter half works without interrupts: an in-flight host-call counter in pinned memory that the watcher reads to decide hot-poll versus sleep, i.e. the watcher stays hot while count > 0 and while a warp is mid-burst. Signal: GPU-maintained outstanding-request counter. Cost: one system-scope atomic per request on the GPU side (cheap compared with the ~10 us service time).
mechanisms.measured: Commit message only ('work will come in large bursts'); no numbers.

mechanisms.name: ROCm (clr) hostcall listener plus device-side s_sendmsg per wave
mechanisms.where: ROCm/clr develop 1c7af0c22797: rocclr/device/devhostcall.cpp HostcallListener::consumePackets() ~285-320, initDevice() ~385 (WaitState::Blocked), kTimeoutFloor/Ceil line 269-270, K = 1000 in rocclr/include/top.hpp:92; device side ROCm/llvm-project amd-staging amd/device-libs/ockl/src/hostcall_impl.cl push_ready_stack()/send_signal() and ockl/src/hsaqs.cl update_mbox() line 69-80
mechanisms.algorithm: Device (default implementation): per wave, the first active lane fills a packet (header.activemask = exec mask, 8 ulong slots per lane), pushes it on a lock-free ready stack, and calls __ockl_hsa_signal_add(doorbell, 1, release). For an interrupt signal that stores event_id into the event mailbox and runs __builtin_amdgcn_s_sendmsg(1 | (0<<4), readfirstlane(event_id & mask)), i.e. one interrupt per wave per call. While waiting for the reply the lane polls its packet with s_sleep(1). Host: a single listener thread loops doorbell->Wait(signal_value, NE, timeout), which is hsa_signal_wait_scacquire(..., HSA_WAIT_STATE_BLOCKED). The timeout starts at kTimeoutFloor = 4*K*K = 4e6 ticks (≈4 ms at ROCr's 1 GHz timestamp). On a value change it halves (floor 4 ms); on a timeout it doubles, capped at kTimeoutCeil = 16e6 ticks (≈16 ms). The timeout only paces the shutdown check, because wake-ups are interrupt-driven. On a wake the listener atomically exchanges the whole ready stack with 0 and serves every packet and every lane in it.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Shows the AMD answer: interrupt per wave, plus a blocked waiter that drains everything per wake (drain-all-per-wake is already our behaviour). Not available on NVIDIA. The part we can borrow is per-wave aggregation on the GPU side: one packet holding all 32 lanes' requests (activemask plus per-lane slots) instead of 32 sequential flag1/flag2 round trips about 9 us apart. That changes what the watcher sees from 32 requests over about 290 us to one request of about 32x10 us of work, so whatever the wake latency, it is paid once per warp, not per lane. Signal: none on the host. This is a GPU-side protocol change (probe codegen or helper).
mechanisms.measured: None in source.

mechanisms.name: ROCr signal wait: 200 us spin (MWAITX) then kernel block (InterruptSignal); opt-in yielding poll 200 us hot, then nap 20->2000 us doubling (BusyWaitSignal)
mechanisms.where: ROCm/rocm-systems develop e4c5ea3acfe9: projects/rocr-runtime/runtime/hsa-runtime/core/runtime/interrupt_signal.cpp InterruptSignal::WaitRelaxed(); core/runtime/default_signal.cpp BusyWaitSignal::WaitRelaxed(); core/util/poll_backoff.h (kPollNapFloorUs=20, kPollNapCeilingUs=2000, kHotPollUs=200, kHotPollActiveUs=10000, NextPollNapUs); core/inc/signal.h DoMwaitx()/WaitForValueChange(); core/runtime/runtime.cpp AsyncEventsLoop ~2097-2323
mechanisms.algorithm: InterruptSignal::WaitRelaxed: loop { check value; if wait_hint == ACTIVE: WaitForValueChange(value, 1000) and continue; if now - start < kMaxElapsed (200 us): WaitForValueChange(value, 60000) and continue; else hsaKmtWaitOnEvent_Ext(event, remaining_ms) (block in KFD until the GPU interrupt) }. WaitForValueChange = MONITORX on the signal's cache line, re-check, MWAITX with the timer enabled (x86 AMD only, g_use_mwaitx); otherwise it returns at once (pure spin) or calls cpu_relax. So it is Karlin spin-then-block with a 200 us spin and a hardware-assisted spin. BusyWaitSignal (no interrupt available), when HSA_ENABLE_YIELDING_POLL=1: spin with MWAITX for 200 us (10 ms if the caller passed HSA_WAIT_STATE_ACTIVE), then os::uSleep(nap) with nap = 20 us doubling to a 2000 us cap (NextPollNapUs), each nap clamped to the remaining timeout. AsyncEventsLoop without interrupts uses the same backoff and resets the nap to 20 us when a wait makes progress. Default is still pure spin, because 'earlier sleep/yield attempts here regressed latency-sensitive workloads' (comment).
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: (1) It confirms our old policy N almost exactly: 200 us hot, then doubling sleeps. ROCr uses floor 20 us, cap 2 ms; ours used 50 us to 1 ms. AMD shipped it opt-in only, for the same latency reason we measured (~530 us mean). (2) MONITORX/MWAITX is the x86-AMD counterpart of our W (WFE plus exclusive monitor) and ROCr bounds it to 200 us before blocking. A W-then-block hybrid follows directly: WFE for at most X us after the last request (X ≈ burst gap plus service, e.g. 200 us), then fall back to M100-style sleep. That keeps W's 14 us latency inside bursts while removing W's 'always runnable' cost between bursts, which is what hurt the full-load case (-14%). (3) The ACTIVE hint widening the hot window from 200 us to 10 ms is the analogue of reading the app's CUDA sched flag: if the app chose CU_CTX_SCHED_SPIN it already accepts a hot core. Signals: time since the last request; cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState flags. Cost on this board: WFE window per burst about 0 extra power (cpuidle off) but counts as running for at most X us per burst; the sleep tail is M100 cost.
mechanisms.measured: No numbers in source; comments cite ROCm/TheRock#7832 (core at 100% for tens of seconds while the GPU is idle) as the motivation.

mechanisms.name: AMD new hostcall: device-side doorbell throttle, at most one interrupt per ~10 us device-wide
mechanisms.where: ROCm/llvm-project amd-staging amd/device-libs/ockl/src/hostcall_impl.cl send_to_host() with SIGNAL_THROTTLE_TICKS 1000 (commit d88ee9ba38, 2026-07-11, PR #3311, guarded by USE_NEW_HOSTCALL_IMPL)
mechanisms.algorithm: Per request, the first lane flips device_phase[i]. Then now = readsteadycounter() (100 MHz). If now - last_signal_time > 1000 ticks (≈10 us), it atomic-exchanges last_signal_time = now and, if the exchange confirms the gap, calls send_signal(doorbell) (interrupt). Otherwise no interrupt is sent. The lane then waits with s_sleep(1) until host_phase[i] == device_phase[i]. How the host catches requests whose interrupt was suppressed is not in this commit (host side not found). Presumably the listener keeps scanning for a while after each wake. UNVERIFIED.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is rate-limited notification: the GPU chooses whether to raise an expensive event, using a device-global timestamp. For bpftime without interrupts, the GPU-side counterpart is a 'last request time' word that the GPU writes into pinned memory and the watcher reads to adapt its period (hot while recent, back off when stale). Cost: one extra relaxed global atomic per request on the GPU.
mechanisms.measured: None (comment: '~10us at 100 MHz steady counter').

mechanisms.name: GENESYS (ISCA'18) GPU system calls: per-request s_sendmsg interrupt, CPU-side coalescing window, work-group granularity
mechanisms.where: Veselý, Basu, Bhattacharjee, Loh, Oskin, Reinhardt, 'Generic System Calls for GPUs', ISCA 2018; arXiv 1705.06965 ('GPU System Calls'), Sec. 3 (coalescing), Sec. 5 (implementation), Sec. 6 Fig. 5/7
mechanisms.algorithm: The GPU work-item, work-group or kernel writes args into a per-work-item slot of a shared 'syscall area', then interrupts the CPU with s_sendmsg. A blocking caller polls its slot state (or halts if hardware allows). The CPU interrupt handler enqueues a kernel task on a Linux workqueue. Coalescing: on an interrupt the handler waits a predetermined time window before enqueuing the task. Requests that arrive in the window are merged into one work item. Two sysfs knobs: window length and maximum number of syscalls per bundle. The paper states that coalescing 'improves system call processing throughput at the expense of latency' and serializes the calls in a bundle. Granularity: work-item invocation is worst ('flood of individual system calls that overwhelm the CPU'), kernel-level gives no parallelism, work-group is the recommended compromise.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Two transferable points. (a) Coalescing window equals our 'after a request, keep polling hot for T': GENESYS makes it explicit and tunable. Our 200 us hot window is the same knob, and their result (a gain only for short calls) matches ours: hot windows pay off only when requests cluster. (b) Invocation granularity: issuing host calls per warp or work-group instead of per lane is the larger lever (see the ROCm hostcall entry). The paper explicitly states its design is 'orthogonal to the interrupt versus polling debate'. Signal: observed inter-request gap in a burst (~9 us), which sets the window: T ≥ a few gaps.
mechanisms.measured: 'system call coalescing can improve performance by as much as 10-15%'; Fig. 7 compares uncoalesced against up to 8 coalesced pread calls (AMD FX-9800P). No CPU-cost numbers.

mechanisms.name: GPUfs (ASPLOS'13) CPU RPC daemon: continuous polling because GPUs cannot signal the CPU
mechanisms.where: Silberstein, Ford, Keidar, Witchel, 'GPUfs: Integrating a File System with GPUs', ASPLOS 2013, Sec. 4.3 (RPC protocol implementation); PDF www.cs.utexas.edu/users/witchel/pubs/silberstein13asplos-gpufs.pdf
mechanisms.algorithm: Quote: 'Today's GPUs also lack a signal-like mechanism accessible to applications, to notify a host CPU process of events originating on the GPU ... do not allow code within a GPU kernel to send notifications. The CPU must therefore poll the GPU-CPU shared memory region continuously to detect RPC requests from the GPU.' Protocol: synchronous, stateless. The request channel is a FIFO in write-shared memory, one per GPU, polled by a single-threaded, event-based host daemon ('to restrict the GPU-related CPU load to one CPU'). Bulk data moves by CPU-initiated DMA into GPU buffer-cache pages, and the CPU then notifies the GPU.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the baseline our watcher descends from (one polling thread, one core). The paper already names the missing primitive, an in-kernel notification, which is still missing on NVIDIA 13 years later (see the Jetson entries). Nothing new to borrow except confirmation that one host thread serving a queue (drain all per wake) is standard.
mechanisms.measured: No polling-cost numbers given.

mechanisms.name: Interference from GPU system service requests (IISWC'18): CPU slowdown from GPU-originated requests; backpressure QoS
mechanisms.where: Basu, Greathouse, Venkataramani, Veselý, 'Interference from GPU System Service Requests', IISWC 2018 pp. 179-190 (dblp conf/iiswc/BasuGVV18); PDF at www2.seas.gwu.edu/~guruv/iiswc18.pdf NOT read (TLS certificate failure; skipping verification was refused)
mechanisms.algorithm: Abstract-level only: GPU requests for OS services (interrupt-driven, AMD APU) slow contemporaneous CPU applications by up to 44%. The proposed fix is a QoS mechanism that dynamically adds backpressure to GPU requests. Exact coalescing or steering constants: UNVERIFIED.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is the published counterpart of our full-load finding: the watcher's CPU time and scheduler interaction slow the CPU load (W -14%). The backpressure idea maps to adapting the watcher to CPU contention: when the box is CPU-saturated, lengthen the period (fewer wake-ups), even though that raises call latency. Signal: the watcher's own run-queue delay from /proc/thread-self/schedstat (2nd field, ns waiting on the run queue) or system load. Note: none of the surveyed implementations uses run-queue delay; that signal would be new.
mechanisms.measured: Up to 44% CPU-application slowdown (abstract). Other numbers unverified.

mechanisms.name: CUDA context scheduling flags (spin/yield/blocking) and the AUTO heuristic, incl. Tegra
mechanisms.where: CUDA Driver API docs, cuCtxCreate (docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-driver-api/group__CUDA__CTX.html); readable at runtime with cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState / cuCtxGetFlags
mechanisms.algorithm: CU_CTX_SCHED_AUTO (flags == 0): with C active contexts in the process and P logical processors, 'If C > P, then CUDA will yield ... (CU_CTX_SCHED_YIELD), otherwise CUDA will not yield ... and actively spin (CU_CTX_SCHED_SPIN). Additionally, on Tegra devices, CU_CTX_SCHED_AUTO uses a heuristic based on the power profile of the platform and may choose CU_CTX_SCHED_BLOCKING_SYNC for low-powered devices.' SPIN: 'can decrease latency ... but may lower the performance of CPU threads'. YIELD: the opposite trade-off. BLOCKING_SYNC: 'block the CPU thread on a synchronization primitive'.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: This is NVIDIA's own three-level answer to the same trade-off, chosen per context, with Tegra defaulting toward blocking (matching our measurement that AUTO behaves as blocking sync on this Orin). Use as a policy input like ROCr's ACTIVE hint: if the app set SPIN, a WFE/hot watcher fits its stated preference. If BLOCKING_SYNC/AUTO (the default here), default to M100-like sleeping. Signal: cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState flags & CU_CTX_SCHED_MASK, read once per context. Cost: 0.
mechanisms.measured: None published.

mechanisms.name: How CUDA blocking sync is implemented on Jetson (nvgpu + host1x): syncpoint increment by the GPU front end -> host1x threshold interrupt -> pollfd wake
mechanisms.where: Local L4T r39.2.1 source: /home/jetson/src/l4t-r39.2.1/Linux_for_Tegra/source/nvgpu/drivers/gpu/nvgpu/hal/sync/syncpt_cmdbuf_gv11b.c gv11b_syncpt_add_incr_cmd(); hal/sync/syncpt_cmdbuf_gv11b_fusa.c gv11b_syncpt_alloc_buf(); common/cic/mon/mon_intr.c nvgpu_cic_mon_intr_nonstall_work(); hal/mc/mc_intr_ga10b_fusa.c ga10b_intr_isr_host2soc_0(); common/fifo/channel.c nvgpu_channel_semaphore_wakeup() ~2376; source/nvidia-oot/drivers/gpu/host1x-fence/dev.c dev_file_ioctl_create_pollfd()/trigger_pollfd() (/dev/host1x-fence is crw-rw-rw-); libcuda strings in /opt/nvidia/l4t-gpu-libs/nvgpu/libcuda.so.1.1
mechanisms.algorithm: Completion is signalled by pushbuffer methods, not by shader code. gv11b_syncpt_add_incr_cmd emits SEMAPHORE methods (sema_addr_lo/hi = the channel's RW syncpoint-shim GPU VA, payload 0, sema_execute = release | optional WFI | 32-bit). A 4-byte release to the shim increments the host1x syncpoint by 1 (get_incr_per_release() = 1). host1x raises a threshold interrupt, and host1x_fence/dma_fence callbacks wake waiters. /dev/host1x-fence exposes HOST1X_IOCTL_CREATE_POLLFD plus TRIGGER_POLLFD {fd, syncpoint id, threshold}, after which poll() sleeps until syncpt >= threshold. libcuda imports poll/usleep/nanosleep/sched_yield and references cuNvRmHost1xWaiterAllocate, cuNvRmHostCreateEventPollFd, cuNvRmHostTriggerEventPollFd, cuNvRmSyncWait and cuNvRmGpuAsGetSyncpointShimRoAddress, which strongly suggests blocking sync waits on host1x syncpoints via pollfd (inferred from symbol strings, not disassembled). Second path: a GR nonstall interrupt (pushbuffer NON_STALL_INTERRUPT method) leads to ga10b_intr_isr_host2soc_0 returning WAKEUP_SEMAPHORE | POST_EVENTS, and nvgpu_channel_semaphore_wakeup() then does an fb_flush and loops over all channels, broadcasting semaphore_wq and posting NVGPU_EVENT_ID_BLOCKING_SYNC (uapi event id 2). The GR 'semaphore pending' interrupt posts GR_SEMAPHORE_WRITE_AWAKEN (id 5). Every trigger above is a front-end method executed between or after work, never by a running SM thread.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: It explains why the GPU cannot wake our watcher mid-kernel through CUDA: every documented wake path is driven by the pushbuffer at kernel or method boundaries. What it does give us cheaply is interrupt-driven kernel-completion notification. Launch tracking can therefore stop polling events every 100 us: record an event created with CU_EVENT_BLOCKING_SYNC after each probed launch and let a helper thread cuEventSynchronize() it (sleeps in poll() on host1x, zero CPU while waiting), then decrement the in-flight count and put the watcher back to deep sleep. This is the piece that 'cost more CPU than it saved' when the GPU is ~100% busy, because the 100 us check becomes 1 wake per kernel. Cost on this board: 1 interrupt plus 1 thread wake per probed kernel. Interrupt-to-userspace latency NOT measured here (plausibly tens of us; nonstall path adds fb_flush plus an all-channel loop).
mechanisms.measured: No published latency for Orin; nothing measured (read-only task).

mechanisms.name: Candidate in-kernel GPU->CPU wake paths on NVIDIA/Jetson (none documented for SM code)
mechanisms.where: (a) CUDA Driver API stream memory ops, cuStreamWaitValue32/cuStreamWriteValue32 (docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-driver-api/group__CUDA__MEMOP.html) + cuLaunchHostFunc (group__CUDA__EXEC.html); nvgpu hal/fifo/pbdma_gm20b_fusa.c gm20b_pbdma_acquire_val() (retry man=2, exp=2); (b) nvgpu uapi include/uapi/linux/nvgpu.h NVGPU_IOCTL_CHANNEL_GET_USER_SYNCPOINT (ioctl 126, gpu_va of RW syncpoint in shim, precondition NVGPU_CHANNEL_SETUP_BIND_FLAGS_DETERMINISTIC) + hal/sync/syncpt_cmdbuf_gv11b_fusa.c ('Create rw map for current channel sync point' in the channel VM)
mechanisms.algorithm: (a) Side-stream trick, documented primitives only: on a dedicated stream enqueue cuStreamWaitValue32(flag_dptr, n, GEQ) and then cuLaunchHostFunc(wake_fn) (or an event record waited on by a CU_EVENT_BLOCKING_SYNC waiter). A running kernel in another stream writes flag >= n to registered host memory. The GPU front end (PBDMA semaphore acquire, acq_circ_geq | switch_en, retry encoded as man 2/exp 2, units unverified) eventually sees it and releases the following work, whose completion goes through the host1x/nonstall path above and wakes a sleeping CPU thread. Requirements: stream mem-op support (query CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_CAN_USE_STREAM_MEM_OPS or v2; support on Orin UNVERIFIED), memory registered via cuMemHostRegister and used through cuMemHostGetDevicePointer (not managed memory), re-arming one wait plus host-func per wake, and the waiting channel must be scheduled concurrently with the probed kernel's channel (same TSG timeslicing; latency UNVERIFIED, could be on the order of a timeslice). Docs warn 'Improper use of these APIs may deadlock'. (b) Syncpoint-shim store from an SM: the channel's syncpoint is mapped RW into the same GPU VM that CUDA kernels use, and the front end increments it with a plain 32-bit semaphore release (payload ignored). An SM st.global to that VA might also increment it and wake a host1x pollfd waiter with a true interrupt. UNVERIFIED on every point: nvgpu_nvhost_syncptshim_map_increment's body is not in the tree (header comment only); CUDA does not expose the VA; GET_USER_SYNCPOINT needs the channel fd owned by libcuda and a deterministic channel; SMMU/permission behaviour for SM writes to the shim is unknown.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: (a) is the only route built from documented APIs to a genuinely sleeping watcher woken by a GPU write. Cost per wake: a front-end acquire/retry plus a host1x interrupt plus a CPU wake, and one re-enqueue (2 driver calls) per wake. Combine it with the in-flight counter: the GPU writes the doorbell only on the 0->1 transition (LLVM rpc pattern) so there is at most one wake per burst. The watcher then hot-polls or WFEs while the counter > 0 and re-arms when it drops to 0. Must be measured (wake latency vs M100's 66-144 us) before any adoption. (b) is research-grade: it needs a prototype with raw nvgpu ioctls and should not go into bpftime.
mechanisms.measured: Nothing measured; all latencies unknown.

mechanisms.name: cudaLaunchHostFunc / cuLaunchHostFunc semantics (what a completion callback costs the app's stream)
mechanisms.where: CUDA Driver API docs group__CUDA__EXEC.html, cuLaunchHostFunc
mechanisms.algorithm: 'The function will be called after currently enqueued work and will block work added after it.' 'The host function must not make any CUDA API calls.' 'must not perform any synchronization that may depend on outstanding CUDA work not mandated to run earlier.' 'Host functions without a mandated order (such as in independent streams) execute in undefined order and may be serialized.' Unlike cuStreamAddCallback, it is not called on a context error. The docs do not say which thread runs it or give any latency figure.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: It suits the 'kernel finished, decrement in-flight' signal (LLVM offload uses it exactly so). Enqueue it on a side stream after cuStreamWaitEvent(side, ev) so the app's own stream is not blocked behind the CPU callback. Host funcs from all streams may be serialized on one driver thread, so keep the callback to an atomic decrement plus a futex wake. Cost: 1 driver-thread wake per probed kernel. Latency unverified on Jetson.
mechanisms.measured: None published.

mechanisms.name: HeteroSync device-side exponential backoff with __nanosleep
mechanisms.where: github.com/mattsinc/heterosync master: cuda/syncPrims/uvm/cudaLocksMutexEBO.cu (lines ~19-52), MAX_BACKOFF in cuda/syncPrims/uvm/main.cu line 7, HAS_NANOSLEEP in Makefile
mechanisms.algorithm: On a failed lock acquire: __nanosleep(backoff) (or a busy for-loop if HAS_NANOSLEEP == 0), then backoff = ((backoff << 1) + 1) & (MAX_BACKOFF - 1) with MAX_BACKOFF = 1024 and initial backoff = 1. Note: the mask makes it wrap rather than saturate once it reaches 1023. Backoff is kept in __shared__ per block.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: GPU side only. While a lane spins on flag2, nanosleep backoff (LLVM rpc uses a fixed nanosleep 64) cuts the polling traffic that the GPU's spinning puts on the shared DRAM/cache path and the coherence traffic on the line the watcher may be WFE-monitoring. Relevant to W: GPU reads of the reply line could cause spurious exclusive-monitor clears/wake-ups, which is UNVERIFIED and depends on whether GPU reads clear the A78AE monitor. Cost: adds up to the backoff value (ns) to the GPU-side reply latency.
mechanisms.measured: None in source.

mechanisms.name: Neutrino (OSDI'25): no live host callback, synchronize and copy probe buffers after the kernel
mechanisms.where: Huang & Wu, 'Neutrino: Fine-grained GPU Kernel Profiling via Programmable Probing', OSDI 2025; preprint open-neutrino.github.io/Neutrino-Preprint.pdf, Sec. 'Runtime Probing' (hook driver)
mechanisms.algorithm: The hook driver intercepts cuLaunchKernel/hipModuleLaunchKernel. It (1) finds the probed kernel, (2) allocates probe buffers from map metadata, (3) 'launches the probed kernel and synchronizes for the finish', and (4) 'memcpys probe buffer back to CPU, then fwrites and frees probe buffers'. 'Callbacks' are posterior Python analysis callbacks, not in-kernel host calls.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Shows that the eBPF-on-GPU tool closest to bpftime avoids the watcher problem entirely by keeping all probe state on the GPU and paying a sync plus memcpy per launch. That supports research direction 1 (GPU-resident per-thread maps/ringbuf): every map op served on the GPU takes one request out of lambda. Neutrino's per-launch synchronize is an app-visible serialization we must not copy.
mechanisms.measured: Overhead numbers in the paper are about probes, not host interaction (not extracted).

mechanisms.name: Per-warp / per-work-group request aggregation on the GPU side (synthesis across LLVM rpc, ROCm hostcall, GENESYS)
mechanisms.where: llvm-project libc/shared/rpc.h (one port per warp; Header{mask, opcode}; first lane does mailbox and doorbell work; rpc::broadcast_value); ROCm ockl hostcall_impl.cl fill_packet() (header.activemask = exec, 8 ulong slots per lane, one push per wave); GENESYS Sec. 6 granularity results
mechanisms.algorithm: Every production GPU RPC protocol surveyed moves requests per warp/wave, not per lane. The warp's active lanes write their arguments into lane-indexed slots of one 64-byte-per-lane buffer, and one lane publishes the packet and (optionally) rings the doorbell. The host serves the whole lane mask and writes per-lane results, then one lane releases the packet. The waiting lanes then broadcast or read their own slot.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: Our measured pattern (a warp's 32 lanes in turn, ~9 us apart) is the per-lane protocol that these systems avoid. With warp aggregation a burst becomes one request, so the watcher wakes once per warp instead of 32 times. Mean latency per lane falls by roughly the 31 extra wake/serialize steps, and both W's preemption exposure and S/M's per-wake cost divide by about 32. This is likely a bigger win than any watcher sleep policy, and it is independent of the policy. Cost: probe-side codegen change (__activemask, __shfl, lane slots). Host-side batch service of up to 32 map ops (~10 us each), which could be parallelized or vectorized.
mechanisms.measured: GENESYS Fig. 5: work-item granularity worst, work-group best (no single number). Not measured for bpftime.

mechanisms.name: GPU-initiated networking (IBGDA / NCCL GIN proxy backend): remove the CPU proxy entirely
mechanisms.where: NVSHMEM proxy.cpp (proxy level NONE when the transport is IBGDA, see the NVSHMEM entry); secondary sources only for latency: emergentmind GDAKI summary, arXiv 2610.01380 'GPU-Initiated Communication: Dissecting Down to the Bone' (NOT fetched), NCCL GIN proxy backend description (summary page, NOT verified)
mechanisms.algorithm: The GPU writes NIC work-queue entries and rings the NIC doorbell itself (IBGDA), so no host thread is needed. The proxy fallback is a CPU thread polling a GPU-written lock-free queue. Secondary claims (UNVERIFIED): the direct path beats the CPU proxy by ~1-2 us for small messages, and a tuned CPU proxy can match it at idle 'at the cost of a dedicated core'.
mechanisms.applies_to_watcher: The analogue for bpftime is to serve the request on the GPU (GPU-resident maps, research direction 1) and keep the CPU only for operations that need the OS. This route avoids the watcher's cost instead of tuning it.
mechanisms.measured: Only secondary-source numbers; unverified.

notes:
The overall answer for bpftime: no surveyed NVIDIA system gives a running kernel a documented way to wake a sleeping CPU thread. NCCL, NVSHMEM, NVBit and GPUfs all poll from the CPU: NVSHMEM, NVBit and GPUfs spin a whole core, while NCCL spins with yield only while ops are posted and otherwise blocks. AMD has one: s_sendmsg into the HSA event mailbox, then a KFD interrupt that wakes hsaKmtWaitOnEvent (used by ROCm hostcall, GENESYS and the LLVM rpc doorbell). Even there, the waiters spin first: ROCr spins 200 us (MWAITX) before blocking.

On Jetson every interrupt path (host1x syncpoint threshold via /dev/host1x-fence pollfd, nvgpu nonstall interrupt leading to semaphore_wq / BLOCKING_SYNC event id 2, GR SEMAPHORE_WRITE_AWAKEN id 5) is triggered by pushbuffer methods at kernel or method boundaries, not by SM code. The one documented-API route that lets a kernel wake a sleeper is indirect: cuStreamWaitValue32 on a side stream followed by a host function or blocking event. Its latency and support on Orin are unverified. The SM-store-to-syncpoint-shim idea is speculative.

Ranked takeaways for the watcher:
1. GPU-side per-warp aggregation, a single request for all 32 lanes, as every production RPC protocol does. It divides wake-ups by about 32 whatever the policy.
2. Replace the 100 us CUDA-event polling with interrupt-driven completion: a CU_EVENT_BLOCKING_SYNC event plus a helper thread, or cuLaunchHostFunc on a side stream (as LLVM offload does). Launch tracking then costs about 1 wake per kernel instead of 10 kHz checks.
3. Bound W in time, ROCr-style: WFE for at most about 200 us after the last request, then M100 sleep. This keeps in-burst latency near 14 us without counting as runnable between bursts.
4. Use the app's CUDA sched flag (cuDevicePrimaryCtxGetState) as a policy hint, as ROCr does with HSA_WAIT_STATE_ACTIVE.
5. Optional backpressure based on CPU contention: no surveyed system uses /proc/thread-self/schedstat run-queue delay, so this would be new. IISWC'18 is the only paper that frames the problem, and only its abstract was verified.
6. Move one-way calls (printk, ringbuf) to NVBit-style batched buffers, to lower the request rate.
